Northwest Georgia power plant has served customers since 1971;

Investments in efficiency and technology include advanced air emissions controls and beneficial reuse of coal ash;

Company building new natural gas units totaling nearly 1,500 MW and 500 MW of battery energy storage

ATLANTA, July 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Since bringing the first unit online in 1971, Plant Bowen has been an essential piece of Georgia Power's diverse generation mix, providing reliable energy for the state as it has grown over the decades, and it has become one of the most advanced coal-fired power plants in the world. Leaders from Georgia Power this week joined the Department of Energy (DOE), as well as elected officials and community leaders, to celebrate the legacy of the plant, as well as the exciting improvements planned and underway as the company reinvests and expands operations at the plant to meet Georgia's growing energy needs. During a ceremony on Tuesday at the plant, the company marked the start of construction of two new combined-cycle natural gas units which will add nearly 1,500 megawatts (MW) of reliable generation. Georgia Power also highlighted its broader investments at Plant Bowen, including a new 500 MW battery energy storage system (BESS) as part of the company's strategy to meet Georgia's growing electricity demand.

The new investments at Plant Bowen are part of Georgia Power's plan to meet increased demand for electricity in the coming years through projects and programs approved by the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC). As the company builds the energy infrastructure needed for a growing state, it remains focused on lowering rates and keeping energy costs stable and predictable. As part of this strategy, in February, Southern Company and the Department of Energy's Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced an up to $26.5 billion loan package to support eligible projects across Georgia and Alabama, including investments in reliable generation, transmission, and grid modernization. The loan guarantee supports projects selected through DOE's financing review process to strengthen America's energy infrastructure while delivering affordable, reliable, and secure energy for the American people. Over the approximately 30-year term of the loans, customers are expected to realize an estimated $7.3 billion in electricity savings.

"For more than 50 years, Plant Bowen has been about more than just megawatts – it has been a source of pride and a cornerstone of the Northwest Georgia community, providing high-quality careers and a positive economic force for this entire region," said Kim Greene, chairman, president and CEO of Georgia Power at the event. "As we celebrate the new investments we're making to serve our customers across the state, and the future of this incredible plant alongside our partners from the Department of Energy and many local, state, and federal officials, we remain committed to making growth work for our customers with higher reliability and lower rates. I'm excited for what comes next at Plant Bowen, and for our entire state, as we continue to work together for a better Georgia for the next generation."

With the approval of the Georgia PSC, Georgia Power continues to expand its diverse generation mix to serve customers and meet growing energy demand with the addition of new natural gas generation, battery energy storage, nuclear uprates, investments in hydropower, as well as transmission system improvements and grid enhancements across the state. In addition to the new units at Plant Bowen, additional natural gas generation projects are planned or underway at sites such as Plant Wansley, Plant McIntosh and Plant Yates, with thousands of megawatts of additional battery energy storage systems also under development, and more than 1,000 miles of new transmission lines planned in the coming years across the state.

Most recently, Georgia Power announced the completion of the Moody Battery Facility, located just outside of Valdosta, Ga., capable of 49.5 MW of battery storage, which can be deployed back to the grid over a four-hour period. This flexible energy storage system matches the output of the nearby Moody solar facility and adds resiliency to the state's power grid. Read more here.

Plant Bowen – as well as Plant Scherer near Juliette, Ga. – are among the most advanced coal-fired power plants in the world, with Georgia Power investing billions of dollars over the decades to reduce emissions and comply with environmental regulations. In recent years, the company has added state-of-the-art technology to reduce the environmental footprint of those facilities such as scrubbers, selective catalytic reduction systems and baghouses. This investment has resulted in reductions in main air emissions by more than 95% over the past few decades.

Additionally, Georgia Power continues to research new and innovative ways to reuse coal ash that are beneficial for customers and communities. The company currently recycles 85% of all ash and gypsum, including more than 90% of fly ash, which it produces from operations for various beneficial uses such as concrete production as well as other construction products. Beneficial use can produce positive environmental, economic and performance benefits such as reduced use of resources, reduced cost of coal ash disposal, and improved strength and durability of building materials. Plant Bowen is currently home to the Ash Beneficial Use Center, a collaboration with Southern Company Research and Development and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), as well as Georgia Power's first beneficial use facility which was the largest of its kind at the time of construction in 2022.

Plant Bowen's Community Impact

Plant Bowen has been a cornerstone and major employer in Northwest Georgia for decades. The plant employs more than 400 people today and Georgia Power expects approximately 1,000 construction workers to be onsite supporting construction of the new natural gas and BESS facilities.

The investment at Plant Bowen is expected to more than double the plant's contribution to property tax revenues in Bartow County. Additionally, Georgia Power, the non-profit Georgia Power Foundation, and individual employees at Plant Bowen have donated hundreds of thousands of dollars in recent years to local organizations with major fundraisers supporting local schools and education organizations, Toys for Tots of Bartow County, foster care programs and local food banks. The Plant Bowen chapter of the Citizens of Georgia Power, a volunteer organization of Georgia Power employees, retirees, and their spouses dedicated to community service, have donated more than 8,000 hours of community service since 2021.

As the plant continues to serve Georgia Power customers, so too are employees at the plant dedicated to serving Euharlee and the surrounding community.

About Georgia Power

Georgia Power is the largest electric subsidiary of Southern Company (NYSE: SO), America's premier energy company. Value, Reliability, Customer Service and Stewardship are the cornerstones of the company's promise to 2.8 million customers in all but four of Georgia's 159 counties. Committed to delivering clean, safe, reliable and affordable energy, Georgia Power maintains a diverse, innovative generation mix that includes nuclear, coal and natural gas, as well as renewables such as solar, hydroelectric and wind. Georgia Power offers rates below the national average, focuses on delivering world-class service to its customers every day and the company is recognized by J.D. Power as an industry leader in customer satisfaction. For more information, visit www.GeorgiaPower.com and connect with the company on Facebook (Facebook.com/GeorgiaPower), X (X.com/GeorgiaPower) and Instagram (Instagram.com/ga_power).

text:
Each week, Walmart serves around 280 million customers across more than 10,900 stores. As one of the world’s biggest retailers, it has significant influence over energy use, procurement decisions and emissions across the wider value chain.

Its FY2026 ESG Report shows how sustainability is now embedded in Walmart’s operating model, shaping energy sourcing, supplier expectations, manufacturing, technology and sustainable investment.

The company is combining renewable energy purchases, supplier collaboration and digital innovation with programmes aimed at improving social and environmental outcomes across its global network.

A focus on resilience

Walmart's ESG Report places sustainability alongside opportunity, community and ethics as one of the four pillars in its shared value strategy, showing that environmental performance is treated as part of long-term business growth rather than a side objective.

The retailer generated US$713.2bn in revenue while operating more than 10,900 stores and eCommerce platforms across 19 countries, supported by around 2.1 million associates. That scale means changes in electricity sourcing, logistics and supplier performance can have an outsized impact on both emissions and energy demand.

The company says strengthening operational resilience, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, cutting waste, protecting natural resources and improving conditions for people across supply chains are intended to lower costs, improve security of supply and build stakeholder trust.

Procurement and supplier relationships remain central to that approach, with Walmart using its purchasing power to push responsible sourcing, sustainable packaging and environmental improvements across manufacturing networks. Technology also plays a major role, with the retailer describing itself as a "people-led, tech-powered" omnichannel business that uses digital capabilities to improve operations and strengthen sustainability across value chains.

“Walmart was built on a simple idea: Help people save money and live better,” says John Furner, President and CEO of Walmart Inc, in the report.

“That purpose still guides us today as a people-led, tech powered omnichannel retailer serving millions of customers around the world each week.

“Our purpose goes beyond providing access to affordable products and services.

“We must invest in our associates, building skills for the future.

“We help our suppliers and sellers reach new markets and grow their businesses.

“Through our people and technology, we are enhancing the sustainability of our operations and our value chains.

“And every day we focus on using our strengths to build the resilience of communities we serve.”

Governance is built into executive leadership and board committees, ensuring ESG priorities influence decision making across the organisation rather than sitting solely within sustainability teams.

Energy transition and decarbonisation

Energy transition remains one of Walmart's most important sustainability priorities, with FY2026 marking a key renewable energy milestone.

“In our operations, we reached our targets of sourcing 50% of our electricity from renewable sources, and we have reduced our absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 24.6% compared with our 2015 baseline year (achieving a 53.7% reduction in emissions intensity over the same period),” says Kathleen McLaughlin, Executive Vice President and Chief Sustainability Officer at Walmart, in the report.

Those gains point to a material shift in how the company powers its estate, with renewable sourcing helping to reduce operational emissions while improving energy resilience and efficiency.

Outside its own footprint, Walmart is also driving decarbonisation through Project Gigaton.

“Suppliers engaged through our Project Gigaton platform reported projects since 2017 expected to avoid, reduce or sequester 1.37 billion tonnes of CO₂e through 2030,” says Kathleen in the report.

The report says climate resilience depends on a mix of renewable energy procurement, lower-emission manufacturing, logistics and agricultural supply chains, reflecting the fact that much of retail’s climate impact sits beyond direct operations. Walmart aligns its emissions reporting with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and receives third-party assurance for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, strengthening transparency for investors and stakeholders.

text:
The California Air Resources Board (CARB) released its 2026 Annual Report on California Climate Investments (CCI) in July 2026, highlighting the continued growth and impact of the state's Cap-and-Invest Program. According to the report, quarterly allowance auctions have generated a cumulative $36.2 billion since the program was launched in 2013. Of this total, approximately $15.5 billion has been appropriated to support 122 climate investment programs across California. While the report focuses on the outcomes of auction revenue investments, it also demonstrates the continued role of carbon market revenues in supporting California's broader climate objectives and the Western Climate Initiative (WCI) framework.

According to the report, CCI funding has supported more than 600,000 individual projects across sectors including clean transportation, energy efficiency, renewable energy, sustainable communities, forestry, agriculture, and climate resilience. CARB estimates that these projects will deliver 130.5 million metric tonnes of lifetime greenhouse gas reductions, highlighting the scale of emissions reductions enabled through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF). The report also highlights continued investment in disadvantaged and low-income communities. CARB reports that approximately 76% of implemented funding, equivalent to $11.4 billion, has benefited these communities through programs such as affordable housing near transit, zero-emission transportation, clean vehicle incentives, urban greening, wildfire resilience, and energy efficiency improvements.

Beyond these investment outcomes, the report demonstrates the growing importance of Cap-and-Invest revenues within California's broader climate strategy. Auction proceeds support a wide range of long-term initiatives, including public transit, clean transportation, forest management, climate resilience, and energy efficiency programs. CARB projects that the program could generate an additional $8 billion in auction proceeds through 2030, highlighting the continued importance of a stable and well-functioning carbon market as a source of climate funding.

The report also highlights CARB's recent amendments to the Cap-and-Invest Program, which are designed to align the program with California's target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2045. Key changes include removing approximately 118 million allowances from future allowance budgets between 2027 and 2030, accelerating the annual cap decline, and requiring one additional allowance to be retired for every offset used for compliance. CARB also introduced complementary measures, including a Manufacturing Decarbonization Incentive reserve and electricity bill credits, to support industrial competitiveness and help manage potential impacts on consumers.

Together, the annual report and recent regulatory amendments mark the next stage in California's Cap-and-Invest Program. The program has evolved beyond a compliance mechanism into an important source of funding for state’s climate priorities, while the latest regulatory changes point toward a progressively tighter allowance market over the coming decade. For regulated entities and other market participants, these developments highlight the importance of incorporating carbon procurement, allowance management, and emissions reduction planning into long-term compliance strategies.

What This Means for Compliance Markets

For participants in the WCI, the significance of the report extends beyond the investment figures themselves. Combined with CARB's recent program reforms, the developments demonstrate that California is strengthening the role of carbon pricing while managing a gradual reduction in available compliance instruments. The increasing reliance on auction proceeds to fund climate programs also creates a strong incentive to maintain a stable and effective carbon market.

However, these developments indicate that compliance entities could operate in a tighter allowance environment through the remainder of the decade. As allowance supply declines and offset flexibility becomes more limited, companies may have fewer options to manage future compliance obligations. This increases the importance of proactive strategies, including forward allowance procurement, allowance banking, and investments in emissions reductions.

Overall, California's Cap-and-Invest Program continues to mature as a long-term carbon market with growing fiscal and policy significance. As the program advances toward its 2030 and 2045 climate targets, carbon pricing is likely to remain an important consideration in compliance planning, investment decisions, and corporate decarbonization strategies.

This summer, plug-in solar legislation continued its run.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Stephan Scherer is an engineer and CEO and founder of Houston-based CraftStrom, which develops and sells plug-in solar systems in the U.S. and Europe. He has testified as a subject matter expert on plug-in solar for statehouses across the country.

With the rising cost of energy plus increased demands from data centers, the momentum for plug-in solar is building quickly.

Utah was the first state to pass a law last year allowing residents to plug solar-generating devices into their homes, and Colorado, Maine, Virginia and other states have followed suit in the span of just a few months.

This summer, plug-in solar legislation continued its run. It passed the California Senate 35-1, thanks to the support of Sen. Scott Wiener. Weeks later, bills passed legislatures in both New York state and New Jersey, now awaiting signatures from their respective governors.

The case for legislation – and attention among policymakers and media – has become apparent and urgent. In the states that have passed plug-in solar laws, residents will be able to save between $175 to $340 every year while reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

With most state legislatures taking a summer break, now is the perfect time to have the conversation about the next wave of proposals.

A new tier of solar supply to meet demand

Energy demands continue to increase while the supply of traditional energy sources has become erratic. And, as air conditioners in households continue to run on high for the summer, rising energy bills have already hit home for millions.

The nation’s energy generation and distribution challenges are all too evident. Aging energy infrastructure, coupled with burdensome permitting and interconnection, means that new electrons often look like they are years — if not decades — away from reaching America’s homes and neighborhoods.

That’s why plug-in solar, also known as balcony solar, legislation has become so popular among lawmakers. Empowering individual households, including renters, to generate their own energy without costly construction or requiring utility approval gives state legislators the opportunity to quickly put money back into their constituents’ wallets.

A recent article from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, published in the peer-reviewed journal, Energies, highlights that utilities “acknowledged that plug-in solar could offer an opportunity to reduce or defer future infrastructure upgrade costs. Plug-in solar has a similar grid impact to utility-scale solar but offers the advantage of being closer to the point of use.”

Like every other new technology, safety questions often come up. In the case of plug-in solar, the issues fall into two different categories: home safety and safety for the utility grid.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

In Germany, more than five million households have already installed plug-in solar without a single incident for homes or their energy infrastructure. Germany became the model for Utah’s state law, which was signed last year, pioneering plug-in solar legislation for the rest of the country.

However, due to differences in Germany’s grid and codes, two issues were lost in translation: appropriate wattage tiers for home safety and clear export limitations for grid reliability.

That could lead to resistance from American utility companies or unnecessarily limit energy savings for American households.

To ensure both household safety and grid reliability, the next wave of plug-in solar state legislation should adopt a two-pronged approach:

Tiered Wattage Definitions: Establish a “safe harbor” tier for systems up to 420 watts that require no complex power control systems, or PCS. Systems exceeding this threshold should mandate PCS for non-dedicated circuits to prevent overloading and ensure NEC compliance.

Export Limits: Cap energy export to the grid at 400 watts. This threshold addresses utility concerns regarding aging infrastructure and reverse power flow, while maintaining the financial benefits for consumers.

Why a 1,200-watt limit doesn’t work

The 1,200-watt cap in Utah’s plug-in solar legislation — which has since been copied in many other states — is an example of how Germany’s specifications don’t translate into success in America. Ironically, it could limit the overall effectiveness of plug-in solar and give false confidence in home safety.

Simply allowing systems up to 1,200 watts without any safety considerations creates unsafe conditions for the home. Most of these systems are not plugged into a dedicated circuit; instead, they are plugged directly into a socket that shares a circuit along with other sockets in the home, known as a “branch circuit,” which has the potential to overload a 15-amp circuit, creating a home fire risk.

In addition, without a PCS, “breaker masking” — where backfed power can reduce the current “seen” by the breaker while allowing upstream conductors to carry more current than the breaker detects — can still happen within the 1,200-watt limit. In that scenario, a section of wiring may overheat without tripping a breaker.

Read More in Renewables

However, when used with a PCS, households can safely use morethan 1,200 watts of energy from a plug-in solar system, so restricting all systems to less than 1,200 watts reduces the effectiveness, and constituent savings, of plug-in solar laws.

The solution for lawmakers crafting plug-in solar legislation is a tiered approach that promotes safe use.

Under this model, a “safe harbor” would be established for systems up to 420 watts, allowing for installation without a PCS while maintaining home circuit safety. Systems exceeding 420 watts would require a PCS for non-dedicated circuits and must adhere to standard NEC regulations for dedicated-circuit setups.

Limiting export to the grid: Increasing reliability for utilities, lowering burdens

After talking to dozens of state lawmakers across the country, from Hawaii to Maine, the question they always ask is: “Okay, but what will our local utility say?”

They are right to ask. Utilities are the key to our energy infrastructure and the common touchpoint for consumers, regulators and legislators. And issues attached to larger residential solar installations, such as net metering and interconnection authorization, can be inaccurately lumped onto plug-in solar.

The answer often surprises them: Technology within plug-in solar can ensure interconnection safety between a home and the grid, and safety for utility lineworkers in the event of a power outage.

By including language in legislation that limits the export of electricity from the home out to the grid to no more than 400 watts, state bill authors and sponsors can find the sweet spot that addresses utilities’ concerns and still saves residents money. This limitation is congruent with the tiered system. As demonstrated in Europe already, the 420-watt safe harbor tier will never export more than 400 watts, and larger systems would be monitored and limited by PCS technology.

Read More in Renewables

Many utilities are justifiably concerned about the reliability of their aging electrical infrastructure. Plug-in solar creates the potential for millions of households now reversing the traditional flow of electricity from the grid to the home, outside of the utilities’ purview. Requiring that plug-in solar systems limit that flow to a negligible 400 watts can reduce the pushback and accelerate passage of legislation.

The absence of explicit export limits in legislation creates a race to the bottom for cheap hardware that puts both households and the grid at risk, an issue we are already seeing in some states. One potential incident – either at a home or for a utility – jeopardizes safety and the widespread adoption of this clean energy resource.

What current state legislation gets right

The building blocks for safe and successful plug-in solar are all here. Now is the time to piece them together, thanks in large part to Utah State Rep. Ray Ward’s successful vision for plug-in solar in his state.

As Jigar Shah and I co-wrote in his LinkedIn newsletter, Accelerating Climate Wealth: “Utah’s 2025 legislation is an important first step. It recognizes plug-in solar as a distinct product category and exempts qualifying systems from utility interconnection agreements when safety requirements are met. The significance isn’t the specific wattage number — it’s the recognition that consumer-scale plug-in generation deserves a different regulatory lane than large export-capable installations.”

And recently, the National Conference of Environmental Legislators outlined three broad provisions for plug-in solar, emphasizing the maturity of the sector and the technology.

Colorado and Maine have already taken the next big steps in their new laws by creating the tiered definitions for plug-in solar, reducing barriers for small systems and underscoring NEC and UL compliance for larger ones. We also suggest following other states and including language that restricts landlords and homeowner and condominium associations from prohibiting households from installing plug-in solar.

text:
A contentious plan to build a behind-the-meter gas power plant to meet growing demand from data centers in Central Washington has been canceled.

The proposed project would have installed 14 gas generators in Quincy, Washington, on land owned by the Grant County Public Utility District. The fuel for those generators would have been delivered by more than a dozen daily semitruck trips. Texas-based energy company VoltaGrid planned to build the facility to meet growing demand from the nearby Vantage data center campus, and the utility approved the plan.

But VotlaGrid’s proposal hit a snag when it sought approval from Washington’s Department of Ecology. The agency planned to approve VoltaGrid’s application for an “air quality notice of construction permit,” the first hurdle a company must clear if it plans to add a new source of air pollution.

When activists got wind that the project was likely to sail through Ecology’s approval process, they began organizing. Washington AI Resistance, the Oil & Gas Action Network, Columbia Riverkeeper, and other environmental groups collected more than 500 comments from Washington residents opposing the project, and submitted them to the Ecology Department. VoltaGrid withdrew its permit application the following day.

“ I was like, ‘That's exciting, and also, what's going on?’” said Valerie Costa, co-director of the Oil & Gas Network. “So is this not going to be built?”

It appears not. Chuck Allen of the Grant County Public Utility District confirmed VoltaGrid does not plan to move forward with the project.

“We understand that the on-site power generation is no longer needed for that location,” he said via email.

Allen said VoltaGrid did not give specific reasons for why the permit was canceled. Neither VoltaGrid nor Vantage responded to questions about the abrupt reversal.

The same day the public comments were delivered to Washington’s Ecology Department, several environmental groups filed notice of intent to sue VoltaGrid in Texas over similar behind-the-meter projects.

The pushback is part of a broader trend of activists and community leaders pushing back on the massive, nationwide data center build out to fuel artificial intelligence. Environmental issues are among the top concerns raised by data center opponents.

“ We're seeing a lot of opposition to the energy facilities tied to data center build-out,” Costa said. “But I think it's really tied to a much deeper existential question around AI's role in our society, in our lives. We are a center of big tech here in Washington state, how big tech is essentially writing the rules for the future, of what it means to be human and how are we going to exist and make a living on this planet.”

title: GM and Ford shift investor conversations away from EVs | Ukraine news - #Mezha
description:

Methodology of the study The TechCrunch study, conducted with Hudson Labs, covers seven years of GM and Ford quarterly earnings calls.
Conclusion Despite the reduced share of EVs in openly discussed investor conversations, GM and Ford continue to develop electric vehicles and related technologies.

The updated Siri AI is already available in the beta of iOS 27 and a broad rollout is planned for this fall.
text:
Over a few years, General Motors (GM) and Ford have radically shifted the priorities in their investments in electric vehicles, and now dialogue with investors is not as active regarding EVs as before. TechCrunch, together with Hudson Labs, analyzed seven years of quarterly earnings calls for GM and Ford and found a decrease in the frequency of mentions of electric vehicles compared with pre-pandemic years.

Although both manufacturers continue to sell electric vehicles and have new models in development, the overall focus has shifted: EVs remain in the portfolio and strategic plans, but their role in investor discussions has diminished amid regulatory and economic shifts.

Shift in GM and Ford’s Focus

GM is pursuing a path toward widespread use of electric vehicles, but the share of mentions of EVs on calls after peak years has decreased. The company emphasizes that changes in regulatory policy and manufacturing decisions affect how time is allocated on calls, as besides EVs they are exploring opportunities in software, services and autonomous technologies, and also discuss regulatory impact, efficiency and capital allocation issues.

quality weighs more than quantity.

– Jim Cain

GM also noted that on the calls they focus on topics of growth in software and services, autonomous technologies, as well as discussing complex topics of interest to analysts and investors – such as the impact of trade and regulatory policy, operational efficiency, capital allocation, regional dynamics and other factors, while giving priority to the Q&A session.

We devote time on calls to discuss growth and opportunities in software and services, autonomous technologies, and discuss the complex topics that interest analysts and investors, such as the impact of trade and regulatory policy, operational efficiency, capital allocation, regional efficiency, obstacles and growth factors – all of this is done so that at least half of the call is devoted to the Q&A session.

– Jim Cain

Ford promotes the concept of the Universal Electric Vehicle as the foundation of its future portfolio and notes that the first production model – a mid-size pickup – is expected to occupy the “golden middle” of the EV market in terms of value, price and technology.

We believe that the first product off the line, a mid-size pickup, will find the golden middle of the EV market in terms of value, price and technology.

– David Tovar

In the context of the overall trend Ford also pointed to further platform development and the potential for scaling electric vehicles, but the emphasis on EV has diminished compared with peak periods, tied to political dynamics and strategic reassessments of investments.

TechCrunch also notes that Stellantis, the third company in the “Detroit Three,” is not included in this analysis for several reasons. The company, formed in 2021 after the Fiat Chrysler and PSA Group merger, has traditionally lagged in the U.S. on EVs and, as of January 2025, held earnings calls not quarterly but twice a year.

Methodology of the study

The TechCrunch study, conducted with Hudson Labs, covers seven years of GM and Ford quarterly earnings calls. The analysis relied on S&P Market Intelligence earnings call transcripts dating back to 2019, and the use of Co-Analyst – a specialized AI tool for financial research – allowed automatic tagging of topics to each sentence and measuring how often topics were mentioned.

According to the analysis, EVs remain part of the portfolio, but their share of discussions about future plans has decreased relative to previous years, indicating shifts in strategy and adaptation to regulatory and economic factors.

Conclusion

Despite the reduced share of EVs in openly discussed investor conversations, GM and Ford continue to develop electric vehicles and related technologies. However, they are not returning to an active focus on EVs with the same intensity as before, but are concentrating on balancing between electric and traditional lines, portfolio management, and regulatory compliance, which shapes the pace and nature of their transition to more sustainable technologies in the future.

During the earnings call on the financial results, Tim Cook said that the long-awaited update to Siri AI could come with certain paid limits. While the details have not yet been finalized, he envisions that users will be able to purchase additional compute resources for Siri AI through existing iCloud+ subscriptions, which provide expanded cloud storage.

We believe there will be many users who want to actively use Siri AI, so we will offer upgrade options through iCloud+ where you can purchase an additional stack of capabilities, and we will see how users respond.

– Tim Cook

Meanwhile, many other AI providers, including Anthropic and OpenAI, operate on a similar model: a free base version with a paid option to increase the limits.

The updated Siri AI is already available in the beta of iOS 27 and a broad rollout is planned for this fall.

Leadership transition and the company’s strategy

John Ternus, long-time senior vice president of hardware, moves into the role of acting CEO after Tim Cook. He will lead the company through a critical period. Apple trails behind competitors in building a sophisticated AI service, even agreeing to use Google’s Gemini licensing model to augment Siri. The delay in the Siri AI update was so significant that the company paid $250 million as part of a deal to market the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Like many hardware makers, Apple is facing rising component costs due to a broader RAM shortage in the market. This is pushing companies such as Meta, Samsung, Microsoft, and Sony to raise prices on individual devices. Last month Apple raised prices for Macs and iPads, but prices for existing iPhone models remained unchanged.

According to industry sources, these factors may influence pricing strategies and the pace of updates, but the exact monetization mechanisms for Siri AI are still being negotiated between company management and service providers.

In short, Apple is considering the introduction of paid limits for Siri AI as part of its monetization strategy, though the final parameters and deployment pace remain uncertain. The company continues to invest in AI development to stay competitive in the dynamic technology market.

text:
Harford County officials and residents say they’re concerned by a proposal to add a utility-scale battery storage facility to a hillside along the “pristine” Deer Creek, a tributary to the Susquehanna River.

Their testimony came Thursday as regulators at the Maryland Public Service Commission reviewed four battery storage projects for eligibility for a new credit, created by state lawmakers in 2025. The other projects are planned on the site of a solar project near Westernport in Garrett County, at the Chalk Point power plant in Prince George’s County and at the former Dickerson coal-fired power station in Montgomery County.

But only the Harford project, a 500-megawatt proposal called the Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project, drew opposition Thursday, with critics citing concerns about fire risk and related environmental contamination.

“Environmentally, you would struggle to find a worse site for this project,” said Jennifer Wilson, a resident who said her children attend the nearby Norrisville Elementary School.

The mostly forested site already hosts Baltimore Gas & Electric’s Conastone Substation, located in the northwestern corner of Harford County. A representative from Tenaska, the company developing the project, said Thursday that the facility would be located at least 600 feet from the waterway, and that most of the 70 acres would remain forested.

Harford County Executive Bob Cassilly (R) also opposes the project, he said in an interview with Maryland Matters, particularly given that the beloved creek — a favorite kayaking spot for him and his family — is located downhill. He worried that firefighters would have trouble fighting any blazes at the site nestled behind the substation, and that any chemicals used for firefighting, or contained within the battery facility itself, would flow down into the river.

“If anything goes wrong with this thing, it goes right down into the Deer Creek,” Cassilly said in an interview. “This is a cherished waterway that feeds the water supply.”

In testimony to the commission, Matthew Kropp, director of Harford County’s planning and zoning department, expressed worries that “toxic heavy metals and chemicals” in the battery infrastructure could leach into the soil or water, and that local fire departments lacked “the training, knowledge and resources to deal with a potential emergency.” He worried that the proposal did not contain sufficient measures to contain a fire or other emergency.

A representative for Del. Lauren Arikan (R-Harford) also said at Thursday’s hearing that her office has gathered 1,300 signatures opposing the project near Deer Creek.

Lee Hine, who lives about a half mile from the proposed project, said he was surprised by its location, given the hilly terrain in a prized natural area.

“The watershed is a prime aspect of why we all moved to this area. It’s a natural preserve here,” Hine said. “I’m trying to understand why we’re not looking for ‘brown ground’ facility areas — or at least flatter areas. This is a mountain. We live on a mountain.”

Keith Latham, who leads battery storage development at Tenaska, said the company plans to use lithium-ion-phosphate batteries, a safer alternative to lithium-ion batteries, and house them in purpose-built enclosures complete with cooling systems.

“Additionally, code standards and best practices have also greatly reduced risk of issues in newer battery storage projects. As we move forward through the development process, we’ll also collaborate with local fire departments and the fire marshal. We’ll work with the first responders on an emergency response plan,” Latham said.

But residents also questioned the project’s cost-effectiveness. A study performed for the PSC found that the Oystercatcher project, the largest by megawatts, did not produce quite enough ratepayer benefit to equal the cost, using two different estimation models.

“I ask the commission to reject this project based on the fact that it doesn’t provide economic relief to BGE ratepayers, and it’s certainly going to put the ecosystem of Harford County at great risk,” Patti Hankins said at the meeting.

Even if one of the projects considered Thursday receives the credits, it still must receive construction approvals from the commission, according to a news release from the commission.

The PSC hearing came hours after a Baltimore news conference, during which environmental groups, unions and a few Democratic politicians extolled the benefits of battery storage technology, which can store extra power for four hours or more and release it to the grid later on. They argued, too, that some safety concerns may be overstated.

Adam Dubitsky, state director for the Maryland Land & Liberty coalition, a conservative nonprofit supporting renewable energy development, said much of the opposition is based on “outdated information about these systems.”

“They are safe when done right, and when firefighters know how to fight these fires — which is very possible — in the rare times when there is an incident,” Dubitsky said.

Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) said any approved project must adhere to the National Fire Protection Association standards, which require separation between battery units to prevent fires from spreading between batteries.

“I understand that when new technology is coming to communities, people are asking questions — totally appropriate for folks to do that,” Charkoudian said during Thursday’s news conference. “It’s just really important that we don’t add to fear-mongering, and we make sure people have the accurate information about the things that keep batteries 100% safe.”

During Thursday’s PSC hearing, John Walser, a fire protection consultant at Fire & Risk Alliance, argued that fires at battery energy sites have become increasingly rare as safety standards have improved.

“This reduction is due to the lessons learned from early failures,” he said, including fires at other battery storage facilities.

At Thursday’s news conference, environmentalists largely focused on the overall benefits of battery storage. It’s particularly important now, they said, as residents face high power bills and the grid faces high demand from data centers and electrification, amid reductions in supply due to the retirement of some fossil fuel generators.

“For most of the history of the electrical grid, if someone flipped on a light switch, a power plant somewhere had to produce those electrons at virtually the same time. But battery storage is changing that,” said Rico Albacarys, political director for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 24. “It allows us to store electricity when it’s plentiful and the costs are less, and then deliver it back to the grid when demand is highest.”

Maryland possesses very little utility-scale, battery storage connected to the transmission grid, Charkoudian said. That’s why the General Assembly stepped in last year with the Next Generation Energy Act, requiring the PSC to open a battery storage procurement for up to 1,600 megawatts. This year, the legislature extended the megawatt limit, as long as cost effectiveness requirements are met.

The facilities can also reduce emissions during high-demand situations, by avoiding the need for fossil fuel “peaker” plants to come online, said Rebecca Rehr of the Maryland League of Conservation Voters.

“Storage reduces reliance on the most expensive, most polluting, and harmful peaker plants that run only during the periods of highest demand,” Rehr said.

Still, the risks concern residents of Norrisville, the small town closest to the Oystercatcher project. Nancy Gladden, who said Thursday she moved to the “blink and you miss it” town in 1984, is concerned that battery projects are unproven, and their safety for the community “highly questionable.”

“We are surrounded by hills and beautiful rolling cornfields and meadows,” Gladden said. “It’s an idyllic place full of homes, happy kids, and wonderful outdoors for them to explore and grow up in. I’m commenting tonight because I’m concerned for the community — for my community.”

title: New York takes on the myth that solar is swallowing farmland - Canary Media
description:
This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter.
In rural areas across the U.S., solar power opponents keep leaning on the argument that utility-scale arrays are gobbling up valuable farmland.
New York’s pushback squares with the findings of a recent report from the Solar Energy Industries Association.
And yet solar panels, not cul-de-sacs, are the focus of a particularly potent campaign from upstate New York influencer Alexandra Fasulo.
(Canary Media)
text:
This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

In rural areas across the U.S., solar power opponents keep leaning on the argument that utility-scale arrays are gobbling up valuable farmland. But plenty of evidence proves that’s just not true, and now, New York is tackling the misinformation head-on.

After the Trump administration accused the state of fast-tracking solar farms on prime farmland, New York leaders fired back last week, saying that renewables ​“empower our farmers to keep their land in use and in their family, while avoiding the threat of permanent conversion or abandonment.” That’s because farmers can lease a plot to solar developers and return it to agricultural use at the end of the array’s life, as the state officials explained in their 11-page letter.

“A recent study by Cornell found that the overwhelming majority of farmers who received solar lease payments used that income to continue or even expand farming on their land, not to exit farming or scale back operations,” the leaders wrote. ​“Discouraging or inhibiting property owners’ ability to independently make choices about what they can and cannot do with their land can cause financial harm and undermine fundamental property rights.”

The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority has more proof that solar and farming can work hand in hand, and outlined all that in a major guidebook it released last year. Sheep and cattle are munching below panels on several New York farms, the guidebook notes, and the state has zoning rules and protections in place to preserve undeveloped land.

New York’s pushback squares with the findings of a recent report from the Solar Energy Industries Association. That study shows solar farms currently take up a mere 0.13% of New York’s roughly 13,000 square miles of federally designated prime farmland, a stat that resonates across the country. Solar covers just 0.07% of all U.S. farmland, according to SEIA. That’s three times less than golf courses and six times less than suburban development.

And yet solar panels, not cul-de-sacs, are the focus of a particularly potent campaign from upstate New York influencer Alexandra Fasulo. Fasulo has amassed more than a million followers across TikTok and other social platforms, where she’s constantly posting videos that inflate solar’s threats to agricultural and undeveloped land. Similar sentiments are being spread on social media by John Rich. He’s one half of the ​“Save a Horse, Ride a Cowboy” guys, and was recently hired by the White House to advocate for landowners on a national scale.

These and other anti-solar advocates often ignore the good that the clean energy source can do for farmers nationwide. In California’s Central Valley, for example, years of drought have led hundreds of thousands of acres of agricultural land to go fallow. Economics and water availability have driven farmers to stop growing there, but they can still make money and hold on to their land by leasing their plots to solar developers.

Plus, as New York’s guidebook points out, farming is still happening alongside solar installations. I recently visited an Illinois solar farm where sheep were grazing underneath and around panels — an arrangement that the sheep’s owners love because they don’t have to maintain expansive pastures back at home. Meanwhile, researchers have found that tomatoes, saffron, and other crops can thrive below panels, and so can native plants.

That’s not to mention the climate benefits of ditching planet-warming fossil fuels, which are driving droughts, floods, and other weather disasters that are legitimately threatening farms in the U.S. and beyond.

More big energy stories

Trump’s coal crusade has real-world consequences

The Trump administration keeps checking items off the coal industry’s wish list — with dire consequences for Americans’ health and wallets.

Over the past year and a half, the federal government has used its emergency powers to keep coal plants from shutting down and pledged $850 million to prop up existing coal facilities or build new ones, Jeff St. John reports. It’s also weakened regulations meant to protect air and water quality, and paved the way for more coal mining in the U.S.

Americans are already suffering the fallout, as Kari Lydersen reports from Indiana. The Department of Energy has forced two aging coal plants there to stay open — a move that is costing plant owners millions of dollars that could soon be passed on to utility customers. Meanwhile, the rollback of federal regulations around coal ash means the toxic byproduct of coal burning will continue to threaten water supplies in the state and beyond.

More data highlights gas stoves’ dangers

Federal funding clawbacks stopped a group of scientists from fully studying gas stoves’ impacts on people with asthma, but they still produced some pretty profound results.

Back in late 2024, researchers from Case Western Reserve University received $18 million from the U.S. EPA to replace gas stoves with electric models in 1,200 Ohio homes whose residents have asthma. Although the grant was canceled a few months into the Trump administration, some people still got their electric stoves — and their asthma symptoms significantly improved.

Gas stoves are risky even for those without asthma. Mixed in with the methane the stoves burn is the cancer-causing carcinogen benzene, along with other toxic pollutants. Those dangers even prompted Colorado to require that gas stoves come with a health warning label — until a federal judge blocked enforcement of the rule shortly after it was implemented.

Clean energy news to know this week

Big money for fusion: Commonwealth Fusion Systems raises another $1 billion from investors, bringing its total funds raised to $4 billion as it seeks to commercialize nuclear fusion technology. (Canary Media)

Courtroom confessions: The Trump administration admits in court documents that it canceled $7.6 billion in clean energy for 16 states solely because those states voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. (Associated Press)

A road map for cleaner factories: It can be hard for factories to justify swapping fossil fuels for more expensive electric power, but a new report suggests that colocating renewable energy generation and reforming electricity rates can help make the case. (Canary Media)

EVs come back around: Global EV sales remained slow in the first three months of the year but rose 35% in the second quarter even amid lackluster growth in China and the U.S., the world’s two biggest EV markets. (International Energy Agency)

Inverters diverted: The Trump administration’s ban on new models of foreign-made inverters, which are critical for connecting renewable power to the grid, won’t impact projects now, but could delay development in the future. (Canary Media)

Electric or bust: California will soon offer hefty rebates to first-time EV buyers, betting on the fact that most drivers who make the switch from gasoline cars don’t turn back. (Canary Media)

title: Certainty for All Energy Projects Will Deliver Abundant Supply, Lower Prices for Ratepayers
description:
Before Congress leaves Washington for August recess, lawmakers must confront one unfinished issue with bipartisan support: energy permitting reform.
Congress has to step in and resolve the permitting reform gridlock permanently to provide certainty for all private sector energy projects.
Businesses, not governments, risk their capital to explore for new resources, develop energy infrastructure, expand production, and transport affordable, reliable energy to consumers.
President Trump reversed this war on fossil fuels, but he needs to improve his approach to renewables, particularly wind energy.
Wind energy has its shortcomings, but calling for the offshore wind industry to be immediately paused is Washington-speak for “shut it down.” Like most other energy projects, delays can be a death knell for wind energy projects.
text:
Before Congress leaves Washington for August recess, lawmakers must confront one unfinished issue with bipartisan support: energy permitting reform.

Negotiators have spent years trying to cut red tape that makes it difficult and expensive to build new power in America. The biggest obstacle is whether presidential administrations should use permitting to favor projects they like and block those they do not. Congress has to step in and resolve the permitting reform gridlock permanently to provide certainty for all private sector energy projects.

Businesses, not governments, risk their capital to explore for new resources, develop energy infrastructure, expand production, and transport affordable, reliable energy to consumers. Creating a stable, predictable investment climate allows companies to make the long-term commitments necessary to meet America’s growing energy needs while strengthening economic and national security.

Unfortunately, federal policies that shift with each new administration creates an uncertain climate for energy investment. The Biden Administration foolishly targeted fossil fuels by canceling pipelines, closing off drilling, imposing new taxes and regulations on oil and gas, and implementing a de-facto ban on natural gas exports. These directives, along with others, clouded the certainty companies need to operate, making energy more expensive over the long-term.

President Trump reversed this war on fossil fuels, but he needs to improve his approach to renewables, particularly wind energy. He’s pulled permits from approved projects with no clear rationale, issued stop work orders, and paused future offshore wind lease sales.

Wind energy has its shortcomings, but calling for the offshore wind industry to be immediately paused is Washington-speak for “shut it down.” Like most other energy projects, delays can be a death knell for wind energy projects.

It’s no surprise, then, that Blue States are suing the administration to get these projects built. Last Friday19 State Attorneys General sued the federal government, saying the offshore wind freeze is illegal and hurts their ability to keep electricity affordable.These lawsuits are ratcheting the pressure on Congress to take action.

No one wins from tit-for-tat energy policy. Projects of this scale are capital-intensive, requiring billions of dollars in upfront costs and often take years—or even decades—to recover. When policymakers signal that a particular energy source will face new restrictions, permitting obstacles, or outright bans depending on which party controls Washington, investors become understandably hesitant.

This creates stranded capital where infrastructure or assets can no longer earn an adequate return because of political decisions rather than market forces. It raises financing costs, leading businesses to delay or cancel investments altogether. Companies made those investments based on the assumption that once they satisfy the law, obtain permits, and survive years of environmental review, they will eventually be allowed to build.

Earlier this year, the Trump Administration pressured a private company to wind down a project off the coast of New York. The company paid the federal government nearly $800 million for the leasing rights and invested hundreds of millions more in infrastructure to build the project. As CEO Patrick Pouyanné bluntly explained, “It’s our money. We gave it in 2022.” Rather than allowing that capital to remain trapped in a politically untenable project, the settlement permits it to be redirected into investments capable of producing actual energy.

Weeks later, Bluepoint Wind, a proposed multi-gigawatt project in the New York Bight, reached a nearly identical settlement with the federal government, agreeing to relinquish its $765 million lease in exchange for redirecting its investment capital into other domestic energy infrastructure.

This phenomenon is hardly unique to renewable energy. The Atlantic Coast Pipeline collapsed after years of litigation, regulatory delays, and ballooning costs. The Mountain Valley Pipeline endured nearly a decade of permit reversals and court challenges before finally entering service after billions in additional costs. Even the Dakota Access pipeline only recently got its final approval after more than a decade of litigation.

A recent study found that nearly one-third of utility-scale solar projects and roughly half of wind projects completing full environmental review later faced lawsuits challenging permits already granted by federal agencies. The National Petroleum Council similarly found that oil and gas infrastructure projects routinely experience multi-year permitting delays that significantly increase project costs.

Congress must act expeditiously. It’s fair to demand fairness across the energy sector, whether it’s a renewable or a fossil fuel project. The sooner Congress addresses this problem, the sooner we can build more projects and lower consumers’ energy bills.

To be clear, if a project is not economically viable and would need massive government subsidies to stay afloat, then it should be cancelled. If a project goes through all the hurdles of a rigorous review and is approved, it should be built.

America needs more electrons on the grid, not more barriers to investment. Yet, our regulatory and political system too often freezes private capital when it is needed most. Congress should enact durable, technology-neutral reforms that provide businesses with the certainty to invest while protecting ratepayers over the long term.

But the following year she said the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was “alarmist”, and some RN politicians have in the past questioned the role of human activity in climate heating.
But since the heatwaves of the start of the summer, key figures in Le Pen’s party have sought to stress that the RN is not a climate crisis denier.

text:
As dozens of forest wildfires burned across France this week amid the summer’s fourth brutal heatwave and increasing air pollution, some wondered whether voters’ first-hand experience of the climate emergency would change the political debate ahead of next year’s presidential election.

The Green leader, Marine Tondelier, who cut short a tour of France on medical advice that at seven months pregnant she should avoid breathing smoke-filled air in the south-west near a huge wildfire in Gironde, said the political class still had its head in the sand.

She said the government had ignored her plea for cross-party crisis talks to declare a national state of emergency on the climate this summer. She called for a new “climate welfare state” in France to help those whose lives were being affected as about 260,000 people were evacuated because of wildfires across the country.

But French politicians focused instead this week on arguments over budgets, crisis planning and criticisms over the levels of state funding for emergency services and equipment to fight fires, including water-bombing planes. The more complex longer-term issues of cutting emissions and structural societal changes to address climate heating were largely left aside.

The president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was not the time to analyse lessons to be learned while France was still in “full battle” against fires.

Macron, whose decade as president comes to an end next spring, returned to his war vocabulary of the 2020 Covid pandemic. As the Gironde wildfire burned an area four times the size of Paris, Macron flew to the crisis operations centre in Bordeaux, saying France was facing its “hardest situation since the second world war”.

He also said the situation was “totally atypical”, suggesting the wildfire was out of the ordinary. Climate experts said growing numbers of forest fires had been predictable amid rising temperatures.

Most political parties will not clarify their full election manifestos – and positions on the climate crisis – until this winter, and some climate campaigners worry that by then the fires and heatwaves may be less present in the media and people’s minds.

Marine Le Pen, who leads the far-right anti-immigration National Rally (RN), is seen as having a good chance of reaching the final round vote in the presidential race. During the second round of the last contest, in 2022, Le Pen said: “I have never been a climate sceptic”. But the following year she said the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was “alarmist”, and some RN politicians have in the past questioned the role of human activity in climate heating.

The RN has also opposed the workings of the EU’s green deal, which is designed to make the EU carbon neutral by 2050. But since the heatwaves of the start of the summer, key figures in Le Pen’s party have sought to stress that the RN is not a climate crisis denier. This week, the RN focused more on the heroism of firefighters and alleged underfunding of fire services by the state than on long-term environmental action.

The radical left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon earlier in July proposed reorganising French regions into “eco-regions” to ensure water supply and deal with the climate crisis.

Rémi Lefebvre, a professor of political science at the University of Lille, said of the current wildfires’ impact on the presidential campaign: “Ecology will probably be talked about more during the election campaign, but I’m not convinced that it will reconfigure French political life.” He said serious wildfires in previous years had not forced a change of direction and French politics had shown itself to be “too short-termist” to dig deep into changing models of society.

Lefebvre said Le Pen did not take a stance of denying climate change “because that is no longer possible … we’ve passed that point”. But he said the broader issue was political inaction on climate challenges. He said a lot of French people felt those in charge were powerless to react.

title: GM and Ford are talking less and less about EVs - Yahoo Finance
description:
General Motors GM bet on mass-market EVs before most other major automakers.
EVs really became a focus of GM's earnings calls as its investment ramped up in 2019 and into 2020.
Ford Ford's first serious entry into the world of mass-market EVs was the Mustang Mach-E, which debuted in late 2019.
Aside from a similar dip in mentions on the Q1 2021 call, which was bogged down by talk of the global semiconductor shortage, Ford — like GM — started spending around a third of each quarterly investor check-in talking about EVs.
Ford began talking less about EVs before the 2024 election, though.
text:
General Motors

GM bet on mass-market EVs before most other major automakers. It debuted the Bolt EV at the Consumer Electronics Show in January 2016, and put the car on sale by the end of that year — a healthy six months or so ahead of Tesla's first deliveries of the Model 3.

EVs really became a focus of GM's earnings calls as its investment ramped up in 2019 and into 2020. At that point, the company was teasing new made-in-the-U.S. models and talking about transforming Cadillac into an all-electric brand. GM spent an increasing amount of time talking about its EV plans through early 2021, with more than 100 references to electric vehicles on each of its last two earnings calls in 2020. That meant EVs accounted for roughly a third of the overall discussion on those calls.

Aside from a dip in the first quarter of 2021, when companies around the world were dealing with a major chip shortage, GM spent nearly the next four years — notably while President Biden was in office — dedicating around a quarter of each earnings call to discussing EVs. (Another notable dip came in the first quarter of 2025 was attributable to President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, which dominated that earnings call.)

After Trump regained office, he slashed environmental regulations that incentivized zero-emissions vehicles, and his party tore up the $7,500 federal tax credit for new EVs. At the same time, GM's talk of EVs dropped significantly, from 82 mentions on the second-quarter call in 2025, to just 21 on its most recent call covering Q2 2026.

While GM remains the second-largest seller of EVs in the U.S., the company that once made the lofty promise to go all-electric by 2035 is now talking more about how it has "align[ed] our EV capacity and manufacturing footprint with the changes in regulatory policy" — when it talks about EVs at all.

Ford

Ford's first serious entry into the world of mass-market EVs was the Mustang Mach-E, which debuted in late 2019. As the company got closer to delivering the first models in late 2020, it started talking more and more about electric vehicles on its earnings calls.

Aside from a similar dip in mentions on the Q1 2021 call, which was bogged down by talk of the global semiconductor shortage, Ford — like GM — started spending around a third of each quarterly investor check-in talking about EVs. Those discussions were buoyed by the launch of its second major EV model, the F-150 Lightning, in 2021. And that level of focus largely held through the Biden years, as his administration freed up federal money for charging stations and EV manufacturing credits, while shaping policy around the battery material supply chain.

Ford began talking less about EVs before the 2024 election, though. By the middle of that year, the company was already backing away from some of its largest contemporary EV investments in favor of a skunkworks project that ultimately became the Universal Electric Vehicle platform. Talk of EVs dipped further after Trump took office, with CEO Jim Farley spending more time discussing support for the president's protectionist trade policy and the company's near-term focus on its higher-margin gas F-Series trucks.

Still, on Ford's most recent call, Farley talked up the idea that the company "will become a major scaled competitor as we invest in affordable, versatile EVs." But for that to happen, investors will have to wait until at least next year.

text:
The billionaires, bureaucrats, and academics make it sound easy.

In his 2021 book Speed & Scale: An Action Plan for Solving Our Climate Crisis Now, John Doerr, the climate activist and Silicon Valley billionaire, claimed that the US could slash its emissions to zero by 2040. Making that happen, he wrote, would require electrifying nearly everything in our society, and “a doubling of the transmission system above business as usual.”

In 2022, Michael Polsky, the billionaire founder of Invenergy, a Chicago-based alt-energy firm that has collected hundreds of millions of dollars in federal subsidies and has repeatedly sued rural communities to try to force them to accept solar and wind projects they don’t want, co-authored an article which claimed that the US “should invest in long-distance, high-capacity transmission lines” and “modernizing” the grid to accommodate more renewable energy. Doing so, Polsky claimed, will “increase reliability” and “send an important message to the world.”

In 2023, the Department of Energy released the “National Transmission Needs Study,” which said that “in future scenarios with moderate load but high clean energy assumptions,” the US will need “a 57% growth in today’s transmission system.”

Also, in 2023, Jesse Jenkins, who heads the Zero Lab at Princeton University, told Utility Dive that by 2035, “we’re going to need to add about 75,000 miles of high voltage transmission lines, enough to run from New York City to Los Angeles and back 15 times...That sounds like a lot for a country not used to building big things. But we have built big things in the past, this is not unprecedented, and shouldn’t be viewed as impossible.”

In 2025, a report by Americans for a Clean Energy Grid and Grid Strategies lamented the lack of growth in the high-voltage grid. It said the US needs to build “roughly 5,000 miles of new high-capacity transmission per year,” to ensure “grid reliability, support economic growth, and deliver low-cost power to customers.”

But as I noted in these pages in 2024, the odds of building such huge amounts of new high-voltage transmission capacity are “as my father used to say, ‘slim and none, and Slim left town.’”

That historical context is relevant because one of the hottest political issues in Texas today (along with the backlash against data centers) is ERCOT’s 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (STEP).

If built, STEP will be one of the largest grid expansions in US history. The project calls for building 2,468 miles of new 765-kV lines, 649 miles of new 345-kV lines, and acquiring (or rather, condemning) about 3,400 miles of new right-of-way. It would also roughly double the amount of 765-kV capacity in the US. But the project, which the Texas Legislature never mandated, is facing fierce opposition. Last month, over 40 Texas state lawmakers signed an amicus brief asking the Public Utility Commission to delay action until the commission “fully evaluates the overall need” for the transmission lines. On Wednesday, I watched a hearing at the Texas Capitol, where more than 200 landowners, including country singer Tanya Tucker, testified before the Texas Senate Business and Commerce Committee. Tucker, who lives on a ranch in Burnet County, told the committee, “I’m very disappointed in how this has been handled. This isn’t the way we do things in Texas.” Tucker was followed by passionate pleas and testimony from ranchers, landowners and officials, all of them opposed to high-voltage lines. The hearing lasted more than 15 hours.

There’s no doubt that the US power grid needs more capacity, and more high-voltage capacity is being built. But a sober look at the STEP project shows that it is little more than a massive cash grab and land grab by some of America’s biggest electric utilities. Further, while big utilities and Texas bureaucrats are claiming the new 765-kV lines will help accommodate more generation capacity and increase reliability, the project provides yet another example of how Texas regulators are bending over backward to connect more weather-dependent generation to the ERCOT grid and, in doing so, saddle ratepayers with billions of dollars in new costs.

Let’s take a closer look.

text:
In early July, the U.S. power grid experienced a heat dome that drove Americans’ energy usage to an all-time high.

There is little doubt that heat waves fueled by climate change, coupled with the rising power use of data centers, will increasingly strain the electrical grid, likely driving up consumer costs even further.

So, what can we do? Virtual power plants offer a real solution where customers can work with power providers to reduce demand for energy and use it efficiently — cutting costs for both consumers and utilities.

At the most basic level, virtual power plants (VPPs) are a network of energy users and suppliers that use existing energy resources in the community and within people’s homes to provide power to the grid—and to strategically reduce energy demand during periods of peak use.

VPPs can be managed by private technology or renewable energy companies, regulated utilities, or other program operators. To manage energy use, VPPs use various devices and technologies that create, store, and use power. This can include rooftop solar, electric vehicles (EVs), home and industrial-scale batteries, smart thermostats, water heaters, and other similar energy systems.

By managing these resources throughout the day as power demand rises and falls, VPPs ensure reliable power while producing energy savings and rewards for participating consumers.

Because they reduce peak power demand and enable a more flexible power grid, VPPs have the potential to reduce or eliminate the need to build expensive and polluting fossil fuel infrastructure.

Preventing these new gas-powered plants from being built eliminates the risk that utility customers, who are already burdened by recent energy rate increases, will be asked to pay for stranded fossil fuel infrastructure as Wisconsin transitions to a clean energy economy.

Particularly as large data centers drive a projected 40 percent increase in energy use by 2032, expanded VPP programs will be necessary to supply reliable power, reduce the health impacts of dirty fossil fuel plants, and keep Wisconsin on track for our 2050 carbon-free energy goal.

VPPs in Your Home

In areas where demand response programs are available, customers can voluntarily install smart thermostats, heat pumps, and other devices in their homes that can be managed remotely by the VPP operator. The operator can then reduce demand and draw excess energy to other users, in exchange for compensating the customers, often via bill credit.

VPP systems have begun to catch on throughout the United States, including in Chicago, where a smart thermostat VPP program was recently approved, slated to begin in May 2027. ComEd, the utility serving northern Illinois, will manage the Chicago program and utilize smart thermostats voluntarily installed by consumers. The program is estimated to save $60 per year for the average household.

So, what would the program look like in your home? Let’s say it’s a particularly hot August day, and your thermostat is set to 70 degrees to keep your house comfortable. A VPP operator may increase your house’s temperature to 73 degrees to reduce energy demand during the afternoon or early evening when energy consumption is high, and the energy grid is under stress.

Making this small change across thousands of homes will significantly reduce energy use and relieve stress on the grid. In exchange, you will receive a bill credit for allowing your thermostat to be remotely controlled.

In 2025, a brutal heat wave hit Vermont. But Green Mountain Power, the region’s utility, sourced power from customers’ batteries distributed across the state, reducing the need to buy expensive peak demand energy. Ultimately, the VPP saved consumers an estimated $3 million in energy costs for just one day — roughly $10 per customer.

RENEW’s Role in the VPP Revolution

Here in Wisconsin, RENEW Wisconsin is working to expand consumer access to rooftop solar systems, making it easier and more financially viable to install a miniature solar energy plant on your property.

Additionally, RENEW advocates for expanded consumer EV and Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) programs that reflect the value of consumers reducing their demand, connecting consumers to the energy system, and enabling customers to exert greater control over their energy — reaping the financial reward when they reduce energy consumption.

Wisconsin’s statewide energy efficiency program, Focus on Energy, provides $50 rebates on qualified smart thermostats across nearly all utilities in Wisconsin. Some utilities also offer demand response programs that are compatible with utility-eligible smart thermostats. These utility smart thermostat programs manage cooling during peak times and provide rewards or bill credits for customer participation.

WE Energies just unveiled a summer program that offers new participants $50 for allowing the utility to adjust their thermostat for up to four hours, with the option for customers to override the adjustment. Returning customers can get more than $6 per month for their participation, shaving a few dollars off their monthly bills.

Another example of a demand response program is WE Energies’ pilot EV program, which gives consumers credit for charging their EVs between 12 am and 8 am, when energy demand is low.

RENEW also advocates for consumers to get monthly bill credits for participating in demand response programs, such as Madison Gas and Electric’s smart thermostat and smart water heater programs. Monthly credits, as opposed to annual bill credits or gift cards, enable consumers to readily see how their participation is reducing energy demand and enabling grid flexibility.

In the future, RENEW will continue to advocate for utilities to make these programs permanent, larger, and more comprehensive — linking together thermostats, EVs, batteries, and rooftop solar to create a smart, responsive energy system for Wisconsin, powered by renewable energy and clean technology.

Doing so will reduce the need for outdated fossil fuel infrastructure, lower customers’ energy bills, and help meet all of Wisconsin’s growing power needs.
