text:
Planet Detroit’s neighborhood reporters are local residents who cover health, environment and climate issues in their neighborhoods. The Lab is made possible with the generous support of the Kresge Foundation.

An outdoorsy kid raised between Catholic schools and Sunday service at her father’s Detroit Baptist church, Tiffany Jones spends her time bridging communities at the intersection of faith and environmental stewardship.

Surrounded by scripture much of her childhood, Jones says environmentalism was rarely discussed.

“There wasn’t anyone there saying, ‘Let’s go outside. Hey, this tree was made by God, y’all!’ But why weren’t these things connecting?” Jones told Planet Detroit.

“I knew that I loved being in nature. I know I found God in nature.”

Today, as the National Wildlife Federation’s director of community engagement for the Great Lakes region, Jones leads Sacred Grounds, a program that helps Detroit houses of worship transform their outdoor space into native plant habitat and rain gardens.

Through building rain gardens, the program works to address stormwater runoff that causes flooding, while creating habitat for birds, bees, and more.

Jones said the program goes beyond green infrastructure to expanding the faith community’s footprint in local sustainability efforts.

“Houses of worship are well-respected and established hubs where people already gather and commune,” she said. “This is just another way to activate those spaces, to do what they already do, but to add another pillar around environmental stewardship.”

Sparking ‘ripple effect’ of gardening

When Jones first moved from Chicago to Detroit as a child, she couldn’t help but notice her new town’s swaths of vacant land. Jones saw spaces with potential to be of great benefit where others saw blight or empty space.

“I had these really big thoughts, specifically around high school, before college, thinking about: ‘What ways we can utilize these spaces to be an asset for communities?’” Jones recalls.

That question guided Jones through her educational and professional journey, from her time as an undergraduate at the University of Michigan, where she studied the relationship between vacant lots, allergenic pollen, and public health. The research pushed her to ask larger questions about how communities manage land and how urban ecology could improve people’s daily lives.

From there, she began to notice parallels between what she learned in environmental science and what she heard throughout her life in church.

Jones said Detroit is prime for the kind of work Sacred Grounds is doing. Detroit’s first church, St. Anne’s Catholic Church, was built in 1701 when the city was settled by French colonists. Now, Detroit boasts hundreds of churches, mosques, shrines, and temples across its 139 square miles.

“Churches are big—they have a lot of property to do these types of projects,” Jones said.

Faith institutions aren’t as big as corporations and industry, “but they cover a lot of land,” she said.

Whether these are small neighborhood ministries or megachurches that draw people from across Metro Detroit, she added, they all have things in common: expansive roofs, large parking lots, and a dedicated group of community members who gather regularly.

It makes them ideal spaces for diverting gallons of stormwater that would otherwise collect on the city’s concrete and asphalt surfaces and contribute to flooding and sewage overflows.

Steve Wasko, executive director of St. Suzanne Cody Rouge Community Resource Center, has witnessed the toll flooding has had on the neighborhood.

“It’ll just drizzle around here, and all the homes on Piedmont Street will report that they got water in the basement,” said Wasko.

The Cody-Rouge neighborhood on Detroit’s west side is at major risk of flooding, according to the climate modeling firm First Street.

Since connecting with Sacred Grounds, a community center tied to the St. Suzanne Our Lady Gate of Heaven Catholic parish has created a neighborhood stormwater infrastructure training program. So far, almost 150 residents have been certified and are maintaining rain gardens throughout the neighborhood, said Wasko.

Wasko, who grew up in the Cody Rouge neighborhood, said he’s noticed the ripple effect the program has on the community: more pollinator gardens and neighborhood curiosity.

“A community member watched us build a couple rain gardens for a few years, and by the third year he came up to me and said, ‘Steve, I’ve been watching what you guys are doing, I’ll build a rain garden in my backyard,’” Wasko said.

“I’m convinced that underlying issues behind flooding and power outages, and all those other things that we are used to in neighborhoods like Cody Rouge, are, at least in part, a result of lack of education, awareness, and employment opportunities that introduce people to these fields.”

‘Social connectivity is a part of environmental justice’

Jones says Sacred Grounds’ aim isn’t to convince communities to care about conservation. Some communities are interested in building habitat, others in reducing flooding and lowering drainage fees. Some want outdoor gathering spaces or educational programming. Some focus on youth, others on older adults.

“The approach that we take is meeting people where they are,” said Jones. “What do you want your community to be? How can we help you get there?”

When Sacred Grounds launched in 2018, the program focused on native plants and wildlife habitats. Then one congregation challenged the program, said Jones.

“They said, ‘We think your programs should stay around, but you’re kind of missing the mark on how you can address issues that are happening in our community, like flooding,’” she recalled.

Sacred Grounds now goes beyond habitat restoration and works to build community capacity around green infrastructure, specifically rain gardens.

Amethyst Crawford manages St. Suzanne Cody Rouge’s education, workforce, and community garden programs. She and Jones coordinated a native plant distribution to engage community members and help reduce flooding.

“We understand that these long root systems that are connected to the native plants help to grab that water and keep flooding down,” said Crawford.

Every native rain garden supports pollinators. But each project is also designed to cultivate something less visible: trust, belonging, knowledge, and the confidence for communities to shape their own future.

“It’s really about giving voice, creating conditions for empowerment for residents to speak for themselves,” Wasko said, “and to do so with some knowledge.”

name: EVs
title: South Africa Proposes Adding Lithium and Other Battery Minerals to Automotive Incentive Scheme
description:
South Africa’s International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC) has proposed expanding the country’s automotive incentive framework to include minerals used in electric-vehicle battery manufacturing, supporting deeper localisation of the domestic automotive and battery-material supply chains.
The proposed framework would recognise 50% of the value of qualifying EV battery materials as local content, potentially improving producers’ eligibility for automotive-sector incentives.
The policy aligns with the South African Automotive Master Plan 2035, which aims to increase vehicle production, local content and investment as the industry transitions toward electric mobility.
SMM comments: The proposal represents a demand-side approach to developing Africa’s battery supply chain, contrasting with Zimbabwe’s supply side policy of restricting concentrate exports to force domestic processing.
If implemented, South Africa could emerge as a regional battery material processing or manufacturing hub sourcing feedstock from neighbouring SADC producers, including Zimbabwe and Namibia.
text:
South Africa’s International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC) has proposed expanding the country’s automotive incentive framework to include minerals used in electric-vehicle battery manufacturing, supporting deeper localisation of the domestic automotive and battery-material supply chains. Under the proposal, the existing list of eligible standard materials including aluminium, steel and platinum-group metals would be expanded to cover lithium, graphite, cobalt, copper, iron and rare earths. Eligible materials would need to originate from member states of the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) or Southern African Development Community (SADC).

The proposed framework would recognise 50% of the value of qualifying EV battery materials as local content, potentially improving producers’ eligibility for automotive-sector incentives. The policy aligns with the South African Automotive Master Plan 2035, which aims to increase vehicle production, local content and investment as the industry transitions toward electric mobility. Stakeholders were given four weeks from the notice date to submit comments, meaning the final scope and implementation schedule remain subject to consultation.

SMM comments: The proposal represents a demand-side approach to developing Africa’s battery supply chain, contrasting with Zimbabwe’s supply side policy of restricting concentrate exports to force domestic processing. If implemented, South Africa could emerge as a regional battery material processing or manufacturing hub sourcing feedstock from neighbouring SADC producers, including Zimbabwe and Namibia.

name: Clean Energy
title: WA Gas Utilities, Meet Clean Heating and Cooling | Sightline Institute
description:
A few years ago, Washington gas utilities looking to decarbonize lacked good options.
That changed when, in 2024, Washington lawmakers unanimously passed House Bill 2131, legalizing gas utilities’ development of thermal energy networks.
Finally, they can require gas utilities to analyze thermal energy networks’ potential as an alternative to pouring ratepayers’ money into the soon-to-be-obsolete, polluting gas system.
Lawmakers could also make grants available to other entities beyond gas utilities, such as electric utilities and municipalities.
Meanwhile, regulators could task gas utilities with analyzing the potential for thermal energy networks as a “non-pipeline alternative” to spending ratepayer money on replacing gas pipes.
text:
A few years ago, Washington gas utilities looking to decarbonize lacked good options. They could pump their natural gas pipes with hydrogen, an expensive and potentially dangerous alternative. They could rely on so-called renewable natural gas, a substance in short supply and with questionable climate bona fides. Or they could offer subsidies for their gas customers to go all-electric, losing those customers—unless the company also sells electricity and does so in the same exact place where it sells gas. Good for the climate, but not exactly a business plan.

That changed when, in 2024, Washington lawmakers unanimously passed House Bill 2131, legalizing gas utilities’ development of thermal energy networks. The law allowed companies to meet their “obligation to serve” customers by furnishing thermal energy (aka, heat or cooling), rather than gas.1 The law also created a thermal energy network pilot program, supported by roughly $5 million in grant funding.2

Thermal energy networks (TENs), which Sightline has written about extensively, are highly efficient heating and cooling systems. TENs in their purest form are distributed networks of ground-source heat pumps that use water-filled pipes to pull heat from the ground (or a water source) in the winter and expel heat in the summer. Because of how efficient they are, thermal energy networks are one of the best and cleanest ways to ease mounting pressure on Cascadia’s grid. They could also offer gas company workers a path into the clean energy economy. Indeed, the United Association of Plumbers, Pipefitters and Sprinkler Fitters, which represents gas utility workers, supported Washington’s TENs bill.

Two-and-a-half years since Washington legalized thermal energy networks, three of the state’s four gas utilities have submitted pilot proposals to regulators at the Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC), and the Washington state Department of Commerce has awarded each utility $1.6 million in grants to offset the project costs. Regulators would be smart to give utilities the chance to pursue a new, clean business line through these pilots, while scrutinizing their budgets.

At the same time, Washington can do more to encourage TENs and try to drive down their costs, the systems’ primary obstacle. Only NW Natural’s proposal is a true-to-form thermal energy network: a distributed system relying on an ambient temperature loop. The other two utilities propose modifying existing campus district energy systems to replace a central fossil gas generation plant with electricity or waste heat—a good idea, but not one that offers TENs’ full grid benefits or learning opportunities. Plus, none of the utilities has committed to pruning its gas system if the pilots succeed.

To fulfill the promise of thermal energy networks, Washington lawmakers could replenish grants for TENs pilots to the $25 million they originally allocated in 2024, with stronger conditions attached to encourage learning and identify ways to shave costs. And even without spending a dime, the state can do more to reduce projects’ sticker shock by directing electric utilities to pay TENs owners for the systems’ benefit to the grid. Finally, they can require gas utilities to analyze thermal energy networks’ potential as an alternative to pouring ratepayers’ money into the soon-to-be-obsolete, polluting gas system.

Pilots spurred by the TENs law would provide efficient heating and cooling to new homes and businesses in Vancouver, WA…

NW Natural’s pilot would provide clean, efficient heating and cooling to three new buildings near the City of Vancouver, Washington’s Columbia River waterfront. The buildings will include some 430 apartment homes and about 28,000 square feet of retail space. Of all three proposals, NW Natural’s hews closest to a true TEN, in that it would be a distributed network of underground pipes filled with ambient temperature water (more on this distinction below).

This thermal energy network would connect to and expand on City Hall’s existing geothermal system, which harnesses energy from an underground aquifer. Underground wells would draw ambient-temperature groundwater and carry it via buried pipes to the homes and businesses. (This water-based model is known as an open-loop system, as opposed to a closed-loop system, which harnesses the temperature of the earth.) Heat pumps in each building would connect to the underground pipes to provide warmth in the winter, cooling in the summer, and hot water year-round.

As a new development, NW Natural’s project will not displace natural gas burned for heat in buildings. Washington’s building code makes electric heat pumps the default heating choice for all new buildings in the state. However, on the coldest winter days, thermal energy networks can be nearly ten times as efficient as air-source heat pumps relying on backup resistance heat. Relying on a TEN for the new development allows the City of Vancouver to lessen the demand of new buildings on the region’s stressed grid, which in the near term also reduces emissions, since Washington’s electricity is not yet fossil-free.

Clark County Public Utility District (PUD), the electric utility that serves the city of Vancouver, submitted a letter to the UTC championing the pilot because of its benefits to the grid.3

The city of Vancouver also enthusiastically endorses the project, stating in a letter of support that it would slash energy use by 36 percent compared with a conventional electric heating and cooling system.4

“Anything we can do to be a good partner and lower energy demand with new development is important for us,” Rebecca Small, the city’s Climate Action Lead and Senior Policy Analyst, told Sightline. Small also noted that the project would help the development meet Vancouver’s Green Building Policy, which will progressively raise energy and emissions standards for new buildings as the city works toward net-zero emissions by 2040.

…and make it possible for two WA colleges to slash climate-warming pollution

Cascade Natural Gas (Cascade) and Puget Sound Energy (PSE), by contrast, both propose retrofitting college campuses’ existing gas-fired district energy systems to rely on cleaner sources.

Neither of these projects meets the precise definition of a thermal energy network. Traditional district energy systems rely on a central plant to generate hot water, steam, or cold water that is then piped to multiple buildings. TENs, by contrast, circulate ambient-temperature water through a looped pipe. Instead of receiving heat from a central plant, buildings connected to a TEN use heat pumps to draw heat from or reject heat into the shared network. This distributed approach allows buildings to offset each other’s energy use (for example, a grocery store could provide heat to its neighbors in the winter), boosting the system’s efficiency. Plus, the networked design makes it possible to connect more homes and businesses over time.

Still, Cascade’s and PSE’s projects would create new opportunities for each campus to decarbonize, as well as provide more cooling.

Cascade’s pilot would connect two Bellingham Technical College buildings to a shared system of water-filled pipes. Like NW Natural’s project, the pilot would rely on groundwater to harness and store heat: in this case, water from the flooded tunnels of the former Bellingham Coal Mine, which operated beneath the campus from 1918 to 1955.

“It’s a giant man-made aquifer about 1,000 feet deep,” Patrick McKinney, Cascade’s Thermal Energy Network Manager, told Sightline.

Electric heat pumps in the buildings would connect to the system to provide heating and cooling. The project backers found that adapting Bellingham Technical College’s existing district energy system, with hot and cold pipes, would cost less than developing a new ambient-loop system.

Cascade estimates that the project will reduce how much natural gas Bellingham Technical College burns by 40 percent. Chad Stiteler, the college’s Vice President of administrative services, told Cascadia Daily News the project would reduce the college’s carbon footprint while giving students hands-on experience with its development.

Similarly, PSE plans to partner with Seattle University to retrofit some of its gas-fired district energy system, heating a student residence and ten other campus buildings (and cooling four of them). The pilot would rely on a central air-source heat pump and allow the university to increase cooling by 30–40 percent, according to Elijah Nerger, Associate Director of Digital Services, who is overseeing the project for the school.

PSE expects Seattle University will burn 60 percent less natural gas because of the project. “We have a campus-wide goal to decarbonize,” Nerger told Sightline. The pilot creates a new opportunity, and one that, he said, makes it possible for the university to meet Seattle’s Building Emissions Performance Standard. The city requires nonresidential and multifamily buildings larger than 20,000 square feet to meet progressively declining emissions targets and reach net-zero emissions by 2050.

“We don’t know how to meet these targets,” Nerger told Sightline. “This thermal energy network project gets us closer, a lot better than what we would be otherwise.”

The projects’ future hinges on their cost

Both NW Natural and PSE are asking regulators to allow them to recover the cost of their TENs pilots from their broader base of gas customers in ongoing general rate cases, the proceedings in which utilities ask for permission to adjust rates. (Cascade’s rate case is also active as of July 2026, but its outcome will be decided after the deadline lawmakers have set for utilities to deploy the TENs pilots.) With the lower-than-expected grant funding from the state, the companies may abandon the projects if they cannot recover their cost in rates, utilities told Sightline.

“It’s a big regulatory question mark,” one of the utilities’ representatives told Sightline.

Together, the companies estimate the pilots’ upfront capital costs (before considering grants or tax credits) to be roughly $54 million: at least $18.5 million for PSE’s Seattle University project, $22 million for Cascade’s Bellingham Technical College project, and $13 million for NW Natural’s Vancouver project.

All three projects would require more upfront investment than maintaining or replacing gas infrastructure. But polluting as usual is not an option if Washington takes seriously its law requiring net zero emissions by 2050. Further, PSE estimates that its pilot would cost $44 million less than an electrification scenario in which Seattle University retrofitted its campus building with individual air-source heat pumps. NW Natural, by contrast, estimates the capital cost of its TEN pilot would exceed an electrification alternative by about $9 million, though the company fails to factor into this figure the TEN’s greater operational efficiency.

In comments to regulators, consumer advocates warned that the utilities relied on partial project designs rather than competitive bidding to estimate costs, leaving the final price tags uncertain. Washington’s Public Counsel noted that PSE stated “actual costs may be materially higher” and questioned whether the projects provide enough public benefit to justify the costs to ratepayers, especially with limited grant funding. A partial settlement agreement between NW Natural; UTC Staff; consumer advocate group, the Energy Project; and the Alliance of Western Energy Consumers would establish a working group to determine whether the utility should move forward with the thermal energy network.

Regulators are right to closely scrutinize the projects’ costs and ensure the utilities take advantage of all available tax credits and grants. The US federal government continues to offer an investment tax credit of up to 30 percent for geothermal projects. NW Natural has also received a credit from Clark County PUD for the projects’ benefits to the grid; regulators could urge PSE to pursue a similar arrangement with Seattle City Light and Cascade with PSE (which provides electricity, but not gas, to Bellingham).

Even so, the project costs could be worth the broader benefits these pilots offer to Washington. Business as usual for both Cascade and PSE means continuing to furnish polluting natural gas to Bellingham Technical College and Seattle University. And all three projects could give the utilities skin in the climate game. Plus, it’s typical for project costs to drop after initial pilots, thanks to economies of scale and learning; Massachusetts utility Eversource expects Phase 2 of the United States’ first utility thermal energy network, in Framingham, to be significantly cheaper than Phase 1, though it hasn’t released precise figures.

Washington can do more to harness TENs’ potential

Even if regulators greenlight the pilots and the projects succeed, Washington may not see more thermal energy network proposals without further leadership from policymakers and regulators.

The primary barrier to thermal energy networks today is their high upfront cost. One way to catalyze more TENs in Washington would be to replenish the $25 million in grant funding that the legislature had planned to allocate to these projects back in 2024. Additional public subsidies to true-to-form TENs will allow Washington to understand how and if these systems fit into the state’s clean energy toolbox—and whether they can follow a learning curve (as with wind and solar) in which more deployment drives down costs. Lawmakers and regulators could set stricter criteria than they originally did for gas utilities to access this funding, including that the project 1) make it possible for gas utilities to decommission gas pipes or mitigate the need to replace them, 2) benefit low-income communities lacking cooling, and 3) rely on high-efficiency, distributed, ambient-loop systems.

Lawmakers could also make grants available to other entities beyond gas utilities, such as electric utilities and municipalities. In 2025, the city of Ann Arbor, Michigan, accepted $11 million in federal grants to develop a thermal energy network that will heat and cool 262 homes, an elementary school, and a community center.

Even absent further grant funding, Washington can do more to encourage TENs. In 2025, Washington allowed the UTC to authorize an electric company to discount electricity rates for the owner of a thermal energy network if it provides certain efficiency benefits. Lawmakers could build on this by directing electric utilities to compensate TENs owners for the systems’ benefits to the grid, formalizing the credit that Clark County PUD proposes offering NW Natural. This type of credit would compensate TENs owners for the systems’ value, driving down project costs and, ideally, eliminating the need for future public subsidies.

Meanwhile, regulators could task gas utilities with analyzing the potential for thermal energy networks as a “non-pipeline alternative” to spending ratepayer money on replacing gas pipes. Sightline estimates that Washington’s gas utilities plan to spend more than $700 million of their ratepayers’ dollars to replace gas pipes over the next several years.5 Massachusetts, the birthplace of utility TENs, again offers ideas. Since 2023, its regulators have required gas companies to show that they considered non-pipeline alternatives (which include TENs)—and found them to be either nonviable or cost-prohibitive—before they can recover costs of gas infrastructure investments.

Thermal energy networks hold tremendous promise for a clean energy transition in Washington that creates good jobs, helps people live more safely and comfortably, and reduces unnecessary electric transmission or generation infrastructure build-out. It’s up to the state’s leaders to make sure that their potential doesn’t peter out.

Thanks to Laura Feinstein and Ricardo Pelai for their research support and feedback on an earlier draft of this article.

text:
BATON ROUGE, La. — Governor Jeff Landry has announced a signed agreement with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) that moves the state of Louisiana into the next phase of negotiations to participate in the federal Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus (NLIC) initiative. This week, DOE Secretary Chris Wright has announced which states have been invited to continue that process.

The concept involves selecting states to host campuses that support activities across the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel and disposition. Additional options include advanced reactor deployment, power generation, and advanced manufacturing, according a spokesperson for the Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy.

The state’s response to the initial DOE invitation was developed using a series of potential functions in the nuclear energy, fuel and support chain and an array of possible sites where those projects might be hosted, including facilities in North, Central and South Louisiana.

“This invitation for Louisiana to advance our nation’s energy security and dominance is a clear sign that our state is well aligned with President Trump’s vision for powering America’s future,” Governor Jeff Landry said. “In launching our Nuclear Strategic Framework, Louisiana signaled we were ready to lead the next era of nuclear energy. This announcement reaffirms our position as a leader in the nuclear renaissance.”

title: How the emerging BESS sector is shaping lithium demand - Fastmarkets
description:
In this feature, Fastmarkets explores the key talking points around the BESS market and its impact on lithium demand and prices.

Access Fastmarkets’ lithium price data, market analysis and forecasting to help you make informed decisions for your business.
text:
The rise in lithium prices in 2026 has led to increased cost pressures for BESS manufacturers and developers.

Fastmarkets’ benchmark assessment of the lithium carbonate 99.5% Li2CO3 min, battery grade, spot prices cif China, Japan & Korea reached a year-to-date peak of $24.50-25.80 per kg on May 12, up by 212% from a recent low of $7.50-8.60 per kg in June 2025.

In this feature, Fastmarkets explores the key talking points around the BESS market and its impact on lithium demand and prices.

Fastmarkets’ experts are embedded in this market, providing price data and market intelligence to help you make sense of today and tomorrow. Stay informed through our news, forecasting and analysis. Find out more about our lithium market insights today.

Growing awareness of lithium price risk management

BESS market participants have sharpened focus on strategies to hedge their exposure to lithium price volatility, following the rise in prices at the start of 2026.

Low lithium prices over the past few years meant that the raw material cost was not a major consideration in the price of BESS systems over that period, market participants told Fastmarkets.

“Our preference is to secure major material sourcing eight to nine months in advance to ensure supply chain integrity,” Nitish Garg, senior director of procurement at ON.Energy, a US-based medium voltage Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) provider told Fastmarkets on Thursday July 30.

“Battery purchase orders are closely managed to optimize the timing between site delivery and commissioning, minimizing storage duration to reduce degradation risk,” Garg added.

Other BESS developers told Fastmarkets that they also have challenges to fix their estimated battery cell costs when bidding or contracting for a new project, with many considering hedging their lithium carbonate exposure, but noting that some banks have scaled back their activity in the sector as a natural counterparty.

In light of this demand for greater flexibility in managing price risk, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) will launch a lithium carbonate options contract, settling against the monthly average of the Fastmarkets lithium carbonate CIF China, Japan and Korea (CJK) price, effective Monday August 17.

A suite of lithium futures and options contracts, including lithium hydroxide and spodumene, which all settle based on Fastmarkets’ assessments, are listed on the CME, Singapore Exchange, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and the London Metal Exchange.

Earlier this year one BESS systems manufacturer told Fastmarkets that while the lithium carbonate price had more than doubled, the effect on BESS system costs was more likely to amount to a 10-15% cost increase.

But other market participants were only concerned about major lithium price swings, comparable to the lithium market in 2021-2023.

“If lithium prices now remain between $20-35 per kg, then I don’t see much necessity to hedge, but if prices spike above $40 per kg, then it can cause an issue,” another BESS market participant said.

Sodium-ion regains focus amid higher LFP cell prices

Sodium-ion batteries have experienced growing interest following the recent increase in lithium prices, but lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells remain the predominant chemistry used in ESS applications, representing “over 90% of the battery energy storage market,” according to the International Energy Agency (IEA)’s Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026.

Previously, barring rapid technological developments, sodium-ion batteries had been expected to take a very limited market share relative to LFP for applications requiring low temperature performance, where it does not have to compete solely on price, in which they still lose out to LFP.

In June 2026, the world’s largest battery maker, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), unveiled its TENER Sodium Energy Storage System, which it described as “field-validated,” adding that “cumulative shipments are expected to reach 1 gigawatt hour by the end of 2026,” with global deliveries to begin in June 2027.

“We believe that sodium and lithium together will form the twin foundations of the future energy storage system,” William Wu, director of CATL’s Energy Storage Technology Center, said.

European BESS provider Alfen plans to deploy 5 GWh of CATL’s advanced sodium-ion battery energy storage systems across Europe, it said on July 16.

Alfen said the decision would allow it to “diversify its battery material portfolio, optimize the cost structure of its energy storage products, strengthen resilience against lithium price volatility, enhancing its competitiveness in mid-to-large scale European project tenders.”

“This new deal expanding into sodium ion battery deliveries to Alfen from CATL for deployment within Europe is a strong indicator for future sodium ESS demand in the region,” Connor Watts, Fastmarkets’ battery raw materials analyst, said.

“Sodium’s superior safety characteristics make it a better option for some smaller footprint applications, while also decoupling these projects from lithium price volatility, even if costs at this point aren’t outright lower than an equivalent lithium ion deployment,” Watt added.

LFP 314 ampere-hours (Ah) prismatic cells remain the mainstream format adopted in BESS. But larger-format cell development is accelerating, with some suppliers moving to 587Ah and beyond, though some concerns remain around cost and the safety of greater energy density.

Fastmarkets published its first China battery energy storage system (BESS) cell price assessment on Friday June 26, expanding coverage further downstream into the energy storage value chain.

Fastmarkets’ first monthly assessment for LFP prismatic cell 314Ah, ex-works domestic China basis was 0.35-0.40 yuan ($0.05-0.06) per watt-hour on Friday. The assessment is published on the last Friday of each month.

Need to stay ahead in the lithium market? Access Fastmarkets’ lithium price data, market analysis and forecasting to help you make informed decisions for your business.

Uncertainty on scale of AI demand clouds ‘behind-the-meter’ BESS demand

Currently, the majority of BESS is being installed “front-the-meter,” which means they are connected directly to the electricity transmission or distribution grid and are typically owned by utilities or independent power producers.

But “behind-the-meter” BESS installations, which are installed on the consumer side of the meter, and thus not connected to the transmission or distribution grid, are growing fast, with many linked to AI data centers.

“Our hyperscaler clients were […] initially reticent and flat out anxious about doing it all behind-the-meter,” Ben Lowe, partner at Roland Berger’s Energy & Utilities practice, told delegates at Fastmarkets Battery & Energy Storage Summit in Las Vegas in June.

“This is the dilemma: either you wait for your interconnection to the grid, or you take it on yourself, and we’ve seen the latter come through in a big way in an extremely short period of time,” Lowe added.

Lowe noted that Roland Berger’s view is that “half of new data centers by 2030 will be off-grid, or at least attempt to be off-grid,” adding that “balancing solar and storage and gas with AI load and other challenges is no small feat.”

Lowe noted concerns about inflated projections of data center power demand across the US, where the majority of data center build-out is concentrated, including for “front-of-meter” demand projections.

“You can look no further than [electric utility provider] AEP Ohio in the last year or so, who had 30-50 GW pipeline of data centers, but then they started to increase financial requirements and commitments for developers to proceed through their transmission approval process, and we saw two-thirds of their queue just disappear,” Lowe said.

According to the Bank for International Settlements’ (BIS) Annual Economic Report 2026, “the five largest hyperscalers are set to spend over a trillion US dollars on AI-related capital expenditure from 2025 through 2026.”

“The intense competition raises the risk of firms over-committing resources to investment projects with still uncertain returns, leaving all firms vulnerable to disappointments in AI payoffs,” the BIS report said. “Disappointment in returns could trigger a sudden pullback in financing and turn the [capital expenditure] boom into a protracted investment bust.”

“[Of the different streams of BESS demand,] AI is the one that you could say has probably the highest chance of a bubble, because it’s difficult to meet the scale of growth that AI is expecting,” Marek Kubik, co-founder of energy storage supplier Fluence, said at the Las Vegas event.

But according to Roland Berger’s Lowe, “even if [AI data center] growth is a fraction of what we’re seeing in projections, that is still an enormous amount of power and infrastructure, and even the hyperscalers themselves don’t know when this ends — their buying habit now is ‘procure as much as you can,’ given supply chains, and use the inventory as a ‘free’ option where and how you want to grow.”

“Our expectation globally is that [data centers] will be the fastest growing segment for storage for the next 5 years — we have data centers at about 25% annual growth, though it’s still a smaller part of the market,” Lowe said.

US policy for localized BESS supply chain needs clarity

US government policy is supporting the diversification of supply chains away from China, but challenges remain for BESS providers to ensure their supply chains are compliant.

“A key piece to the tax credits 45X and 48E is this new prohibited foreign entity [PFE] guidance that will need to come out and how they’re applying that and requiring industry to show compliance,” Emma Bishop, vice president at consultancy Venn Strategies, said.

In the US, 45X is an advanced manufacturing tax credit, set to be phased out in 2032, and 48E is a clean electricity investment tax credit, phasing out entirely in 2036.

“You have a tax credit for critical minerals, then you have a tax credit for electrode active materials, then cells & modules, also for battery energy storage systems — that is unique to this industry and something you don’t see elsewhere,” Bishop said. “How are they thinking about Safe Harbor tables, defined per each of those segments in the supply chain, so you have true continuity and clarity for industry as they apply?”

Safe Harbor is the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) framework that determines whether a clean energy project can qualify for various federal tax credits.

“It is important to distinguish between two separate policy mechanisms: the Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC/PFE) restrictions and the Domestic Content Investment Tax Credit (ITC) requirements. There is overlap in some requirements but these operate independently and should not be treated as a single compliance framework,” ON.Energy’s Nitish Garg said.

“On a cost-by-cost basis, Chinese cells are likely to be cheaper, but with the credits and additional policies, I think they can be more neck-and-neck [with domestic production or PFE-compliant production],” Garg added.

In the near-term, reliance on Chinese supply of cells into the US is likely to continue as the domestic US supply chain continues to develop.

According to US import and export statistics published by the Census Bureau, China-origin imports of lithium-ion batteries (HTS number 850760) totaled 35.88 million units over January-May 2026, falling by 52.89% year on year from the corresponding period in 2025.

Amid US government policy changes since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025, including the termination of consumer tax credits for EVs, a number of South Korean and Japanese companies with US investments have been pivoting from EV battery cell production, converting US production lines to produce ESS cells.

Market participants have also noted that a lack of coordinated policy support regarding the high cost of building out ex-China midstream lithium processing infrastructure remains a key barrier to building out an independent ex-China supply chain.

Trump’s EPA just decided that if a power plant exists solely to supply a data center, it is exempt from the Acid Rain Program. That means it no longer has to comply with the program’s limits on sulfur dioxide emissions, even though the pollution is exactly the same.

Congress created the Acid Rain Program in 1990 because sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides don’t stay where they’re emitted. They travel downwind, fall as acid rain, damage lakes and forests, and worsen asthma in communities that may be hundreds of miles away.

Nothing about that science changes because the electricity is sold to one customer instead of many.

EPA is trying to create this exemption while avoiding Congress. But agencies cannot rewrite statutes by memo. If Congress intended to exempt privately dedicated power plants from the Acid Rain Program, we would have written legislation to do so. We most certainly have not.

EPA is attempting to narrow a law Congress enacted without Congress’s approval. Courts should reject it, and Congress should make clear that clean air protections apply based on pollution, not on who buys the electricity.

text:
Haldimand County will receive $500,000 from Ontario Power Generation to help "explore opportunities" for new energy production at the former Nanticoke coal-fired plant, as the province considers bringing electricity generation back to the site over a decade after it was shut down.

The "growth readiness funding" will allow the municipality and OPG to begin community consultations and planning for new "firm" energy generation, including the possibility of small modular reactors (SMRs), the province announced Wednesday. Firm energy refers to electricity that can be produced reliably on demand, unlike wind or solar power.

While no decision has been made on what technology will ultimately be built, Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said hydrogen, natural gas and nuclear are the leading options.

"We've not made any decisions on technology. That will only follow meaningful engagement," Lecce told a news conference in front of transmission infrastructure at the site of the Nanticoke facility, once the largest coal-fired plant in North America.

The announcement is the latest step in Ontario's push to expand electricity generation. The province says demand for electricity is expected to increase by as much as 90 per cent by 2050.

Former coal plant offers 'jewel' of a site

Lecce said Nanticoke is uniquely positioned for a new power project because much of the infrastructure is already in place.

The 364-hectare property is already zoned and permitted for up to 3,000 megawatts of electricity generation, and has access to high-voltage transmission lines, rail service and a port.

"This is a jewel of land, and it's unacceptable it has not been delivering value," Lecce said.

He said while natural gas could be built within a few years, an SMR would likely take closer to a decade.

The funding will also allow Haldimand County and neighbouring communities to better understand what different projects could mean, said Kim Lauritsen, OPG's senior vice-president of enterprise strategy and growth.

"We have not made a decision about what generation type," Lauritsen said. "The funding allows the community to have the capacity to understand how we need to plan for that."

Haldimand County Mayor Shelley Ann Bentley said the money will be used to educate residents, engage neighbouring municipalities and Indigenous partners, and gather feedback before any decisions are made.

"We'll use these funds to get this conversation started in a positive manner."

Bentley said she hopes to see new energy generation on the site within five to 10 years.

Former plant worker says site deserves 2nd life

For Haldimand Deputy Mayor Deborah McKeen, Wednesday's announcement was also deeply personal.

McKeen spent 27 years working at the Nanticoke Generating Station after becoming the plant's first female maintenance mechanic in 1986. She was among the workers who left when the station closed in 2013.

"My reaction to today's news is absolutely ecstatic," she said.

She recalled a workplace with strong camaraderie and a sense of pride in supplying electricity during periods of peak demand across Ontario.

"We knew we were important to the province. We were supplying hydro, and we were proud to do it."

McKeen said the site already has infrastructure that would take years and billions of dollars to replicate elsewhere.

"Basically, we have a diamond sitting here. We need to showcase it and put it back in service for the province."

Province says project could bring thousands of jobs

The plant, which was closed under the former Liberal government, was Ontario's largest coal-fired power plant and, for years, the province's single biggest source of air pollution.

A federal report found that in 2000, it emitted 7,640 tonnes of toxic pollutants — more than the combined total of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

The Kathleen Wynne government made ending coal power a keystone of their policy.

Lecce acknowledged there was "virtue in decarbonizing," but criticized the previous government for not doing enough to replace the long-term jobs lost when the plant shut down.

"This community faced a great deal of hardship," he said.

While he would not estimate how many jobs a future Nanticoke project could create without first selecting a technology, Lecce pointed to the four SMRs planned at Darlington as an example. He said those projects are expected to create between 18,000 and 19,000 construction jobs and about 3,700 permanent jobs.

"Eighty per cent of small modular reactors are sourced using made-in-Canada, made-in-Ontario components."

Haldimand County Council passed a motion in 2024 in support of nuclear energy in Nanticoke. The county has had a moratorium on wind power development in place since 2013.

Business leaders say a major energy project would benefit the wider region, not just Haldimand.

"Major energy projects of this scale and potential create broad regional opportunities," said Renée VanKooten, president of the Simcoe and District Chamber of Commerce.

"This is more than an energy project. It is a catalyst for prosperity across both counties."

text:
The U.S. solar market continues to navigate complex regulatory adjustments and shifting trade landscapes midway through 2026. Following months of policy uncertainty, pricing for domestic solar module assembly has settled at a median of $0.30 per watt, holding flat through May, June, and early July, according to newly released data from procurement platform Anza.

The current baseline of $0.30/W reflects a minor rebound from $0.295/W in April, down from $0.31/W recorded in the first quarter of the year. Pricing across the 55 U.S.-assembled modules tracked by Anza spans an interquartile range (P25 to P75) of $0.280 to $0.325 per watt, reflecting varying risk profiles, cell sourcing locations, and tax credit eligibility features.

FEOC rules spark structural divestments

Tightened Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) rules under the “One Big Beautiful Bill” (OBBB) act have triggered a wave of corporate restructurings across U.S. module manufacturing.

Under current Treasury rules, any manufacturing facility where a designated FEOC holds more than 25% equity, where multiple FEOCs collectively hold over 40% equity, or where FEOCs hold over 15% of outstanding debt risks classification as a Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE). Projects relying on modules manufactured by a PFE face losing access to Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) Investment Tax Credits (ITC).

To preserve project eligibility for domestic buyers, major Chinese-headquartered manufacturers have undertaken structural asset sales:

Trina Solar transferred its Wilmer, Texas assembly facility to FREYR (rebranded as T1 Energy), converting its involvement to intellectual property licensing and long-term supply arrangements.

JA Solar completed a 100% equity sale of its 2 GW Phoenix facility to Corning Inc., which now operates the site as American Panel Solutions.

JinkoSolar divested a 75.1% controlling stake in its Jacksonville, Florida plant to FH Capital for $192 million, retaining a 24.9% non-controlling minority interest.

LONGi reduced its equity stake in the Pataskala, Ohio Illuminate USA joint venture facility below the critical 24.9% threshold.

Industry observers note that while direct legal ownership has changed, significant portions of the underlying equipment, ingot, and wafer supply chains remain tied to overseas parent companies, leaving long-term regulatory interpretations open.

New AD/CVD petition targets South Korea

Trade uncertainty expanded beyond Southeast Asia on June 18, 2026, when the American Manufacturers for Energy Resilience (AMER) coalition filed an Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Duty (AD/CVD) circumvention petition targeting solar imports from South Korea. The coalition—comprising Jeffersonville PV Cells Corp. (Canadian Solar), SEG Manufacturing, and Heliene USA—alleges that Chinese-origin processing in South Korea is minor and insufficient to alter the country of origin.

The petition primarily targets operations tied to Hanwha Q Cells, alongside HD Hyundai and Shinsung E&G. The U.S. Department of Commerce is scheduled to decide on initiating the investigation on July 9, 2026. Preliminary CVD determinations are expected in September 2026, with preliminary AD determinations following between November 2026 and January 2027, introducing potential retroactive tariff liabilities for developers using Korean-sourced cells.

Segment breakdown and sourcing dynamics

TOPCon technology accounts for the vast majority of U.S. assembly capacity, representing 49 of the 55 module products in Anza’s U.S. assembly index, with legacy mono PERC filling the remaining slots. Tier-1 status applies to 45 of the modules, while 32 meet current FEOC cell compliance criteria.

Cell origin for U.S. module assembly remains highly fragmented across ten countries, led by Kenya (12 modules) and the Philippines (11 modules). Polysilicon supply for these modules is primarily sourced from Malaysia (24 modules), followed by the United States (15 modules) and China (13 modules).

Looking ahead to 2027

With the threshold for non-PFE components required for domestic content eligibility set to rise to 45% for projects beginning construction in 2027, procurement teams face rising friction between hardware availability and tax credit compliance.

Anza advises developers to move beyond self-certifications by implementing independent third-party supply chain audits and legal opinions to verify FEOC status. Furthermore, buyers utilizing South Korean cell imports are urged to audit upstream wafer and ingot origins to hedge against potential AD/CVD duty retroactive enforcement.

text:
Ford is seeking to expand its business beyond vehicle production, including pursuing more U.S. military contracts.

The company won a prototype contract to compete against GM Defense and BC Customs to build the U.S. Army's next tactical vehicle.

CEO Jim Farley stated Ford is focused on adjacent businesses that are close to its core operations.

Ford Motor is seeking more projects related to the U.S. military as well as considering creating other adjacent businesses outside of its core business, vehicle production and car sales, to add to its future revenues, CEO Jim Farley said.

Farley made the comments on July 28 during a second-quarter earnings call with Wall Street analysts, just hours after Ford confirmed it won a prototype contract to compete to build the U.S. Army’s next tactical vehicle, known as an Infantry Squad Vehicle (ISV), based on its F-Series Super Duty pickup.

Beyond making vehicles for the U.S. military, Ford also has started a new venture building battery energy storage systems at its plants that make electric vehicle batteries in Kentucky and Marshall, Michigan. On May 18, Ford Energy, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of Ford, said it signed a five-year "framework agreement" with EDF power solutions North America to make battery energy storage systems for EDF.

When analysts asked Farley to outline Ford's vision as to where it can go in doing work for the Defense Department or by creating other side businesses, Farley said the automaker is considering expansions in both areas. He said Ford continues to discuss additional defense-related projects with the U.S. government.

"We do believe we have a lot to offer; we’ll think through this as an adjacency," Farley said. "It has to be a strong business with really good returns. When you look at the scale of the opportunity here and all the opportunities versus something like (battery energy storage systems), which has a very short payback, they’re pretty different opportunities. They’re very asymmetric."

U.S. Army outlines Ford's competition

The competition is fierce in both defense and battery energy storage systems businesses. In battery storage systems, competitors such as Tesla have a big head start on Ford, though experts argue Ford has the right technology and a competitive edge with its partner, Chinese battery maker CATL.

In the case of the U.S. military contract, it's potentially a lucrative opportunity for Ford if the company wins the production contract to build the vehicle.

U.S. Army spokesman David Patterson told the Detroit Free Press on July 29 in an email that the U.S. Army awarded the Other Transaction Authority (OTA) prototype contract to two other companies in addition to Ford: GM Defense and BC Customs, an off-road vehicle manufacturer and defense contractor that specializes in custom tactical vehicles, chassis fabrication, and specialized trailers.

"Each of these three vendors is contracted to build and deliver three prototypes of the ISV-H (Infantry Squad Vehicle Heavy)," Patterson said in an email. "These prototypes will go head-to-head in physical and operational testing before a production contract award."

Patterson said GM, Ford and BC Customs were each awarded $3.33 million to deliver the three prototype ISV-H vehicles and their respective logistics package. He said that each carmaker must deliver their three ISV-H systems to the Army in March 2027 and the Army will conduct comprehensive testing on all nine prototypes to evaluate their capabilities, reliability and performance.

By late fall of 2027, the Army will make a decision on which company wins the business. Farley said Ford stands a good shot because it has vehicle platforms, technologies and capabilities already established to provide the military with global service and parts support.

"We already dominate in that market in the commercial world," Farley said. "We want to offer the U.S. government the same advantages that our commercial customers get. That includes great parts availability and everything else that comes along with being the leader."

GM Defense's hope to win more

But GM also has a lot of off-road vehicle experience in recent years. In 2017, GM formed the subsidiary GM Defense to apply its vehicle technology to military equipment in hopes of winning lucrative government contracts with U.S. and foreign governments.

GM Defense won its first contract, worth $214.3 million, in 2020 to build the ISVs for the U.S. Army. It has won other contracts since then. In 2021, GM Defense won a $36.4 million contract from the U.S. State Department to develop large support utility commercial vehicles for the department’s Diplomatic Security Service, which is the federal law enforcement and security arm of the department.

On July 21, GM CEO Mary Barra told Wall Street analysts that if Congress appropriates the funds, the company stands to win a $1 billion contract to build military vehicles off the Chevrolet Colorado frame. She also said that GM Defense revenue will grow to nearly $700 million this year and it is on target to achieve positive earnings before interest and taxes. In the next several years, Barra said, GM Defense will produce double-digit profit margins.

Patterson said the contract Ford is competing for is different from the $1 billion contract Barra referenced.

"The $1 billion figure represents the potential cumulative value of the U.S. Army’s long-term procurement objectives for the baseline Infantry Squad Vehicle program, should all future options and annual appropriations be fully funded," Patterson said. "The current ISV-Heavy prototype contract is separate from the baseline ISV production contract."

Still, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said Ford wants a piece of the pie that GM Defense has been eating from for nine years.

"Ford is going after this golden goose opportunity and following GM’s path," Ives told the Detroit Free Press. "This is a smart move and there are many adjacent monetization opportunities on the defense front for Ford."

Ford's other opportunities

Farley told Wall Street on July 28 that Ford also is focused on pursuing adjacent businesses that are "very close to our core business, like battery energy storage systems and defense."

"There’s a few others that we haven’t talked about yet," Farley said. "They’re not all the same, and they don’t all have the same opportunity."

When asked what to make of Farley's elusive remarks, Wall Street autos analyst David Whiston said Ford has side business opportunities available now like never before such as software service subscriptions or subscriptions to its hands-free BlueCruise driving system.

"It’s good option value in investing parlance and batteries for energy storage makes a lot of sense if Ford can’t use that capacity for EVs," Whiston said.

text:
A proposal for a federal program to protect the Mississippi River is in front of Congress for another time.

Spearheaded by U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, the Mississippi River Restoration and Resilience Initiative is modeled after the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, a popular and bipartisan program that has spent more than $4.5 billion since 2010 to address threats to the Great Lakes basin.

The river also needs this kind of investment, Baldwin contends, as it faces continued pollution and threats from invasive species. More extreme cycles of flooding and drought also affect the communities that live along it, as well as those who ship goods on the river to and from the central U.S. and other parts of the world.

“As communities along the river face more frequent flooding and worsening pollution, we must confront these challenges head on while also making the long-term investments needed to prepare for those ahead," Baldwin said in a July 28 news release.

First introduced in 2021 by U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum of Minnesota and again in 2024 with Baldwin's backing in the Senate, the bill has thus far failed to find Republican support to move forward, despite the endorsement of dozens of groups that advocate for the river. McCollum is again authoring the companion bill in the House.

A spokesperson for Baldwin said the senator is engaging with river communities, nonprofits, municipalities and potential bipartisan cosponsors to promote the concept of the Mississippi River program.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency would implement the program, according to the bill text, working with federal and non-federal entities to draft an action plan to improve the ecological health of the river. Projects would focus on improving water quality, restoring habitats, reducing the presence of invasive species and creating natural infrastructure to protect against flood damage.

The program also would create three research centers along the river corridor to study such issues.

One change in the newest version of the bill is the inclusion of the Hypoxia Task Force as an entity that is required to be consulted on the action plan for the river. The task force was established in 1997 to reduce the size of the Dead Zone in the Gulf of Mexico (renamed by the U.S. government as the Gulf of America), which is a low-oxygen area that chokes off plant and aquatic life. Estimates show this summer's Dead Zone could be roughly the size of New Jersey.

The bill text states that the work of the river program may not "supplant the functions" of the task force.

McCollum's initial version of the bill would have appropriated about $300 million annually to support the program, which was dropped for its 2024 reintroduction. At the time, she told the Journal Sentinel that removing the appropriations language could be a necessary change to bring some lawmakers on board.

Slow progress on the Mississippi River program reflects a markedly different political environment than when the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative was formed, river advocates have told the Journal Sentinel.

Though President Donald Trump proposed gutting funds for the Great Lakes initiative during his first term, Democrats and Republicans alike in Congress rebuffed the move. In March, the U.S. House passed legislation to reauthorize the initiative through 2031. It is still awaiting Senate passage and Trump's signature.

title: Technology Innovation Story - Technologies for the Electricity Era : Hitachi Global
description:
Ohashi: Countries pursuing electricity reform face shared challenges stemming from the growth of renewable energy and the democratization of energy systems driven by electricity market liberalization.
My sense is that getting the balance right between generation capacity (kW) and energy generation (kWh) will prove a very difficult challenge.
The electricity systems of the past achieved security of supply by investing large sums in transmission networks.
A system for trading electricity supply four years ahead based on a target for how much capacity will be needed at that time.
